  "$schema": "https://developer.microsoft.com/json-schemas/sp/v2/column-formatting.schema.json",
  "elmType": "div",
  "attributes": { "class": "=if(@currentField == '', 'sp-field-severity--warning', '')" },
  "txtContent": "=if(@currentField == '', 'Missing', @currentField)"
}
  For a choice column use @currentField; for a person column test length(@currentField) == 0 and show @currentField.title.

Stop new gaps
  Make the column required, or set default values per folder (Library settings > Column default value settings).

Chase owners (monthly flow)
  Get items where MetadataComplete eq 0, group by Created By, and email each person their files with a link to the view.
stepByStepInstructions: Check the columns the filter needs exist, and add an index to each one used in the filter.
Create a new view from All Items and give it a name that says what it shows.
Decide which columns count as required for good content.
Filter for each key column equal to an empty value, joined with OR on small lists.
On large lists, use one indexed column per view or a MetadataComplete flag maintained by a flow.
Open the view in grid edit and fill the gaps in bulk.
Share the view's URL, or pin it as a tab in the team's Teams channel.
commonMistakes: An OR filter on a list above the view threshold.
Making columns required without fixing existing gaps, which blocks edits to old items.
Chasing metadata nobody uses.
troubleshooting: If the view errors on a large list, split it by column or use the indexed flag.
If a managed metadata column cannot be filtered for empty, use the completeness flag.
If files stay checked out to the uploader with missing required properties, they are invisible to others until properties are completed and the file is checked in.
If the flag flow loops, check the trigger condition compares the stored flag with the calculated value.

create-a-sharepoint-view-for-high-priori.shortDescription: Build a view of open high and critical issues, sorted so the most severe and oldest are at the top.
create-a-sharepoint-view-for-high-priori.fullDescription: High priority issues deserve their own view, shown on the team's home page and in stand-ups. The detail that matters is making priority sort in order of severity and keeping the view to open issues only.
create-a-sharepoint-view-for-high-priori.problemStatement: Critical issues are scattered through a long list, sorted alphabetically between High and Low, and get no more attention than minor ones.
whenToUse: Issue, defect, incident and risk lists
Daily stand-ups and escalation reviews
A list web part on a team or project home page
whenNotToUse: Lists where nearly everything is marked high, which needs a priority reset first
Incident management with paging and on-call, which needs a dedicated tool
create-a-sharepoint-view-for-high-priori.formulaOrCode:
Columns needed
  Priority     Choice    1 - Critical | 2 - High | 3 - Medium | 4 - Low        indexed
               (the number prefix makes sorting and grouping follow severity)
  Status       Choice    New | In progress | Blocked | Resolved | Closed        indexed
  AssignedTo   Person    DueDate  Date      Created  built in

View: High priority open issues
  Filter : Status    is not equal to   Closed
           AND
           Status    is not equal to   Resolved
           AND
           Priority  is less than      3              (text comparison: matches "1 - ..." and "2 - ...")
  Sort   : Priority ascending, then Created ascending
  Columns: Priority, Title, AssignedTo, Status, DueDate, Created

  If the less-than comparison is not offered for your choice column, use two views
  (Priority = 1 - Critical, Priority = 2 - High) or add PriorityRank (Number) set by a flow:
    Filter : PriorityRank is less than or equal to 2         (indexed number)

Existing choices without numbers (Critical, High, Medium, Low)?
  Add PriorityRank (Number): Critical 1, High 2, Medium 3, Low 4, maintained by a flow or the form.
  A calculated column works for display and sorting but cannot be indexed for large lists:
    =IF([Priority]="Critical",1,IF([Priority]="High",2,IF([Priority]="Medium",3,4)))

Priority pill (column formatting on Priority)
{
  "$schema": "https://developer.microsoft.com/json-schemas/sp/v2/column-formatting.schema.json",
  "elmType": "div",
  "style": { "padding": "2px 10px", "border-radius": "12px", "display": "inline-block", "font-weight": "600" },
  "attributes": {
    "class": "=if(indexOf(@currentField, 'Critical') > -1, 'sp-field-severity--blocked', if(indexOf(@currentField, 'High') > -1, 'sp-field-severity--warning', 'sp-field-severity--low'))"
  },
  "txtContent": "@currentField"
}

Related views
  Critical only            : Priority = 1 - Critical AND Status not Closed, not Resolved
  High priority, unassigned: add AssignedTo is equal to (empty)
  High priority, overdue   : add DueDate < [Today]

Put it in front of people
  Team home page : List web part > this view > hide command bar
  Teams          : add the list as a tab and choose this view
  Alert          : Automate > Create a rule > "When a column value changes" (Priority) > notify the team lead
                   or a flow that posts to the channel when Priority becomes 1 - Critical

Keep high meaningful
  Define each level in the column description, for example "1 - Critical: service down or data at risk".
  Review the share of high and critical items monthly; if it passes about 20 percent, recalibrate.
stepByStepInstructions: Check the columns the filter needs exist, and add an index to each one used in the filter.
Create a new view from All Items and give it a name that says what it shows.
Prefix priority choices with a number so they sort by severity, or add a numeric rank column.
Filter to open statuses and to the top two priority levels.
Sort by priority, then by Created ascending.
Format the priority column as a coloured pill and add the view to the team's home page.
Share the view's URL, or pin it as a tab in the team's Teams channel.
commonMistakes: Priority choices that sort alphabetically.
Including resolved issues, which buries the open ones.
Letting most issues drift to high priority.
troubleshooting: If Critical sorts after High, the choices have no numeric prefix. Add a rank column.
If renaming choices leaves old items with the old text, update existing items in grid edit.
If the view is slow on a large list, put the indexed status or rank condition first.
If the pill formatting shows plain text, check the JSON is applied to the Priority column in this view.

govern-required-fields-by-lifecycle-stag.shortDescription: Require different columns at different stages of an item's life, using list validation, forms or an app.
govern-required-fields-by-lifecycle-stag.fullDescription: A SharePoint column is either always required or never. Real processes need a cost centre at approval and a resolution at closure, not at creation. This pattern shows three ways to enforce stage-based requirements and when to use each.
govern-required-fields-by-lifecycle-stag.problemStatement: Marking a column required blocks people from saving a new item, and leaving it optional means items reach Closed with nothing filled in.
whenToUse: Lists with a status or stage column
Fields that only make sense later in the process
Rules that must hold however the item is edited
whenNotToUse: Columns that are needed from the start, which should simply be required
Complex rules across related lists, which need a flow or app
govern-required-fields-by-lifecycle-stag.formulaOrCode:
Define the rules first
  Stage           Must have
  Submitted       Title, Category, Requester
  Approved        + CostCentre, ApprovedBy
  In progress     + AssignedTo, TargetDate
  Closed          + ResolutionNotes, ClosedOn

Option 1: list validation (enforced everywhere: forms, grid edit, Power Apps, flows)
  List settings > Validation settings
  =AND(
     IF(OR([Status]="Approved",[Status]="In progress",[Status]="Closed"), NOT(ISBLANK([CostCentre])), TRUE),
     IF(OR([Status]="In progress",[Status]="Closed"), NOT(ISBLANK([TargetDate])), TRUE),
     IF([Status]="Closed", AND(NOT(ISBLANK([ResolutionNotes])), NOT(ISBLANK([ClosedOn]))), TRUE)
   )
  Message: "Fill in the fields required for this status: Approved needs a cost centre;
            In progress needs a target date; Closed needs resolution notes and a closed date."

  Limits: one formula and one message per list; about 1,024 characters;
          cannot reference person, lookup or managed metadata columns; multi-line text only as ISBLANK.

Option 2: conditional forms (guides the user in the SharePoint form)
  Open an item > Edit form > Edit columns > column menu > Edit conditional formula
  Show ResolutionNotes only when closing:
    =if([$Status] == 'Closed', 'true', 'false')
  This shows and hides fields. It does not make them required, so pair it with Option 1.

Option 3: Power Apps (clearest messages, works with person and lookup columns)
  DataCard.Required : ddStatus.Selected.Value in ["In progress", "Closed"]
  Or validate on save:
    If(ddStatus.Selected.Value = "Closed" && IsBlank(Trim(txtResolution.Text)),
       Notify("Add resolution notes before closing", NotificationType.Error),
       SubmitForm(frmRequest))
  The app does not stop edits made in the list. Keep Option 1 as the backstop.

Option 4: a flow that reverts invalid changes (for columns validation cannot read)
  When Status = In progress and AssignedTo is empty: set Status back and notify the editor.

Help people before they hit the rule
  Column descriptions: "Required before closing."
  A view "Incomplete for stage": items whose status needs a field that is empty.
stepByStepInstructions: Write down which columns each stage requires.
Leave the stage-dependent columns as not required in column settings.
Add a list validation formula that checks each stage's fields.
Use conditional form formulas or a Power App to show the right fields at the right time.
Add a view that lists items missing fields for their stage, and use a flow for person and lookup columns.
commonMistakes: Marking late-stage columns as required, which blocks new items.
Relying on a Power App alone when the list can be edited directly.
A validation message that does not say which field is missing.
troubleshooting: If the formula is rejected, it references a column type validation does not support, or exceeds the length limit. Move that rule to an app or flow.
If existing items cannot be edited after adding validation, they already break the rule. Fix them in grid edit with validation off, then turn it on.
If flows start failing, their Update item steps now break the rule. Set the required fields in the same update.
If users cannot tell what is wrong, list each stage's needs in the validation message.

govern-list-owners-and-backup-owners.shortDescription: Make sure every important list has a named owner and a backup, recorded in one place and checked regularly.
govern-list-owners-and-backup-owners.fullDescription: Lists outlive the people who made them. A register of lists with an owner and a backup, a rule that both are filled, and a regular check against leavers keeps accountability from quietly disappearing.
govern-list-owners-and-backup-owners.problemStatement: A list that runs a process breaks, and the only person who understood it left the organisation a year ago.
whenToUse: Sites with lists that support business processes
Departments with several makers
Before a reorganisation or after staff changes
whenNotToUse: Personal lists
Sites with a single list and an obvious owner
govern-list-owners-and-backup-owners.formulaOrCode:
Register: List Owners (one row per governed list)
  Title            Single line    list name
  ListUrl          Hyperlink
  Site             Single line
  Purpose          Multiple lines
  Criticality      Choice         Business critical | Important | Convenience          indexed
  PrimaryOwner     Person                                                               indexed
  BackupOwner      Person                                                               indexed
  OwningTeam       Choice
  UsedBy           Multiple lines apps, flows and reports that depend on it
  LastConfirmed    Date           when the owners last confirmed they still own it      indexed
  NextConfirmation Date                                                                 indexed
  Status           Choice         Active | Ownership gap | Retiring | Retired

What an owner is responsible for
  Deciding who has access            Approving column and view changes
  Data quality and retention         Knowing what depends on the list
  Responding to problems, or naming who does

What a backup does
  Has the same permissions and knowledge, and covers absence. Not a name on paper only:
  they should have made at least one change or run through the support notes.

Rules
  Business critical lists need both owners filled and from the same or a neighbouring team.
  PrimaryOwner and BackupOwner must be different people (check in a flow; validation cannot read person columns).
  Owners need at least Edit on the list; the register entry does not grant it.

Views
  Ownership gaps      : BackupOwner is empty OR PrimaryOwner is empty
  Confirmation due    : NextConfirmation <= [Today]+30
  By owner            : group by PrimaryOwner       (what does this person own?)
  Critical lists      : Criticality = Business critical

Checks (monthly flow)
  1. For each row, look up both owners:
       Office 365 Users - Get user profile (V2); a failure or accountEnabled = false means a leaver
     Set Status = Ownership gap and notify the owning team's manager.
  2. NextConfirmation reached: email both owners "Do you still own <list>?" with Yes / Hand over options.
     Yes -> LastConfirmed = today, NextConfirmation = +6 months.

When someone leaves or moves
  Search the By owner view for their name, agree a new owner for each list, update permissions,
  and walk the new owner through the dependencies.

Show ownership on the list itself
  List description: "Owner: <team>. Contact: <shared mailbox>."
stepByStepInstructions: Create a register with one row per important list, including purpose and criticality.
Record a primary owner and a different backup owner for each.
Write down what owners are responsible for and make sure they have the permissions to do it.
Add views for ownership gaps and confirmations due.
Run a monthly check for leavers and a six-monthly confirmation with both owners.
commonMistakes: Treating the list's creator as its owner for ever.
A backup who has never opened the list.
Recording owners but not checking whether they are still in the organisation.
troubleshooting: If the gap view is slow, it uses OR. Create one view for each empty column.
If the leaver check fails for guests or shared mailboxes, exclude those or handle the error in the flow.
If nobody will take ownership, raise it with the business area. An unowned critical list is a risk to record.
If owners change often, record the owning team and a shared mailbox as well as individuals.

govern-lookup-reference-list-changes.shortDescription: Control changes to lists that other lists look up to, so renaming or deleting a value does not break records, apps or flows.
govern-lookup-reference-list-changes.fullDescription: A reference list is shared infrastructure. Deleting a row can blank the lookup on thousands of items or block the deletion, and renaming changes what every dependent record displays. This pattern sets rules for adding, renaming and retiring values safely.
govern-lookup-reference-list-changes.problemStatement: Someone tidies a departments list, and the next day historical requests show the wrong department or none at all.
whenToUse: Lists used as the source of lookup columns
Reference lists read by Power Apps and flows
Shared values such as departments, locations and categories
whenNotToUse: Choice columns, which are changed in column settings
Reference data mastered in another system and synchronised
govern-lookup-reference-list-changes.formulaOrCode:
Know what depends on the list
  List settings > each lookup column in other lists points back to it. Find them:
    Get-PnPField | Where-Object { $_.TypeAsString -like "Lookup*" } | Select Title, LookupList      (per list)
  Also record: apps that load it, flows that filter on its values, Power BI reports.

Design the reference list to be changed safely
  Title        the display value (may be renamed)
  Code         a stable key that is never changed                 unique, indexed
  IsActive     Yes/No, default Yes                                indexed
  SortOrder    Number
  ReplacedBy   Lookup to the same list, for merges
  ValidFrom / ValidTo   optional dates

Rules for each kind of change
  ADD      Safe. Add the row. Apps that cache reference data show it after a restart.
  RENAME   The lookup shows the new text on every existing item, including historical ones.
           Fine for corrections ("Finanse" to "Finance"). For a real change of meaning, add a new row and retire the old.
           Check flows and formulas that compare on the text, e.g. Department eq 'Finance'.
  RETIRE   Set IsActive = No. Never delete a value that has been used.
           Apps and lookups should offer only active rows:
             Power Apps: Filter(Departments, IsActive = true)
             SharePoint lookup column: cannot filter natively; use a Power App form, or accept that
             inactive values are selectable and prefix them "(retired)".
  MERGE    Add ReplacedBy on the old row, update existing items in bulk (grid edit or a flow), then retire it.
  DELETE   Only for rows never used. Deletion behaviour depends on the lookup's relationship setting:
             Restrict delete : SharePoint blocks deletion while items reference the row (safest)
             Cascade delete  : deletes the referencing items too (rarely what you want)
             None            : the lookup on those items becomes empty
           Set it under the lookup column's settings > "Enforce relationship behavior" (the column must be indexed).

Change process
  1. Request: what change, why, and from when.
  2. Impact check: count items using the value (filter a view or Get items with a filter).
  3. Approve: the reference list's owner.
  4. Apply, then check one dependent app, one flow and one report.
  5. Log it in a Reference Data Changes list: Value, ChangeType, RequestedBy, ApprovedBy, Date, ItemsAffected.

Protect the list
  Permissions: Read for everyone, Edit for data stewards only.
  Versioning on, so a mistaken rename can be seen and reversed.
  Column description on Code: "Do not change. Used by apps and flows."
stepByStepInstructions: List every list, app, flow and report that depends on the reference list.
Give the reference list a stable code and an active flag.
Set rules: add freely, rename only for corrections, retire instead of delete.
Set the lookup columns' relationship behaviour to restrict delete.
Limit editing to data stewards and log each change with its impact.
commonMistakes: Deleting a value that historical records use.
Renaming a value that flows compare by text.
Letting every site member edit the reference list.
troubleshooting: If a lookup shows blank on old items, its target row was deleted. Restore it from the recycle bin within 93 days.
If deletion is blocked, restrict delete is doing its job. Retire the value instead.
If a flow stopped matching after a rename, change its condition to use the stable code or the lookup Id.
If a retired value still appears in the SharePoint form's dropdown, native lookups cannot filter. Use a customised form or mark the title as retired.

govern-document-library-default-metadata.shortDescription: Set default column values on a library and its folders so documents are tagged automatically when they are uploaded.
govern-document-library-default-metadata.fullDescription: People skip metadata. Column defaults, including per-folder defaults, fill it in for them: a file dropped into the Contracts folder gets Document type Contract and Department Legal without anyone typing. This pattern covers how to set, govern and check them.
govern-document-library-default-metadata.problemStatement: Documents arrive with empty metadata, so filtered views, search refiners and retention rules that depend on it do not work.
whenToUse: Libraries where folders already reflect a category, department or project
Bulk uploads and drag and drop
Metadata that drives views, search or retention
whenNotToUse: Values that differ for every file, which need the user or a flow
Libraries with no folders and a single default for everything, where a simple column default is enough
govern-document-library-default-metadata.formulaOrCode:
Two levels of default
  1. Column default (whole library)
     Library settings > column > Default value
       DocumentStatus = Draft        Confidentiality = Internal        ReviewDate = [today]+365 (calculated default)

  2. Per-folder default (overrides the column default for that folder and below)
     Library settings > Column default value settings
       select the folder on the left > click the column > "Use this default value"
       /Contracts         DocumentType = Contract     Department = Legal
       /Contracts/NDAs    DocumentType = NDA          (Department inherited from the parent)
       /Finance/Invoices  DocumentType = Invoice      Department = Finance

What gets a folder default
  Files uploaded, dragged in or created in that folder, and files synced in through OneDrive.
  Not: files already in the folder, and files MOVED in with existing values (moves keep their values).
  Supported: text, choice, number, date, person, managed metadata. Not supported: lookup, multi-line, Yes/No in some cases.

Plan it
  Folder                 Column            Default        Owner
  /Contracts             DocumentType      Contract       Legal ops
  /Contracts             RetentionCategory 7 years        Records manager
  /Projects/<code>       ProjectCode       <code>         PMO (set by the provisioning flow)

Set defaults in bulk or by script
  PnP PowerShell:
    Set-PnPDefaultColumnValues -List "Documents" -Field "DocumentType" -Value "Contract" -Folder "Contracts"
  For new project folders, call the same from a provisioning flow or Azure Automation runbook.

Backfill existing files
  Open the folder in a view > Edit in grid view > fill down. Or select all > details pane > bulk edit.
  Or a flow: Get files (properties only) limited to the folder > Update file properties where the column is empty.

Check it is working
  View "Missing metadata": DocumentType is equal to (empty).  Should stay empty for folders with defaults.
  Spot check: upload a test file to each configured folder after any change.

Govern it
  Only library owners change defaults. Record each default and its reason in the library's documentation.
  Review when folders are added, renamed or restructured: defaults are tied to the folder path,
  and a renamed folder keeps its defaults but a recreated one does not.

Alternative without folders
  A flow on file creation that sets metadata from the file name, the uploader's department or the content type.
stepByStepInstructions: Decide which columns can be derived from where a file is stored.
Set library-wide defaults in each column's settings.
Set per-folder defaults under Column default value settings.
Backfill existing files in grid edit or with a flow.
Record the defaults, restrict who can change them and re-test after folder changes.
commonMistakes: Expecting defaults to apply to files already in the folder.
Setting defaults on deep folder trees that are later reorganised.
Forgetting that moved files keep their old values.
troubleshooting: If uploads do not pick up the default, check the folder path in the settings matches after any rename, and that the column type is supported.
If a managed metadata default does not apply, re-select the term in the settings. Term defaults are stored by ID.
If defaults apply in the browser but not through a flow's Create file, set the properties in the flow with Update file properties.
If the settings page is missing, Column default value settings appears only for libraries, not lists.

govern-site-page-retirement-dates.shortDescription: Give site pages a retirement or review date and act on it, so outdated pages are updated, archived or removed on schedule.
govern-site-page-retirement-dates.fullDescription: Pages written for a project, event or old process stay published long after they are wrong. A retirement date column on Site Pages, a view of what is due and a simple retire routine keep an intranet trustworthy.
govern-site-page-retirement-dates.problemStatement: Search results surface pages about a system replaced two years ago, and staff follow instructions that no longer apply.
whenToUse: Intranets and department sites
Pages about time-limited topics such as projects, events and campaigns
Sites with many authors
whenNotToUse: Sites with a handful of evergreen pages
News posts, which are dated by nature and can be handled by audience and age
govern-site-page-retirement-dates.formulaOrCode:
Site Pages library: add columns
  PageOwner        Person                                                       indexed
  PageType         Choice    Evergreen | Time-limited | Policy | Project | Event
  RetireOn         Date      when the page should be reviewed or taken down      indexed
  RetireAction     Choice    Review and extend | Archive | Delete | Redirect
  RedirectTo       Hyperlink replacement page, when there is one
  PageState        Choice    Live | Review due | Retired                         default Live, indexed

Defaults by page type (set when the page is created, or by a flow)
  Event        : event date + 30 days       -> Archive
  Project      : project end + 90 days      -> Archive
  Policy       : + 12 months                -> Review and extend
  Evergreen    : + 24 months                -> Review and extend
  Time-limited : author chooses             -> Delete

Views on Site Pages
  Retiring in 60 days : PageState = Live AND RetireOn <= [Today]+60, sort RetireOn
  Past retirement     : PageState <> Retired AND RetireOn < [Today]
  No retirement date  : RetireOn is equal to (empty)
  Retired             : PageState = Retired

Monthly flow
  Get files (properties only), Site Pages
    Filter Query : PageState eq 'Live' and RetireOn le '@{addDays(utcNow(), 30, 'yyyy-MM-dd')}'
  For each page: set PageState = Review due and email the PageOwner:
    "<Title> is due to be retired on <date>. Planned action: <RetireAction>.
     Extend it (set a new Retire on date), or leave it and it will be retired."

Retire routine (owner or site manager, for pages past the date and not extended)
  Archive  : move the page to a /SitePages/Archive folder and unpublish it
             (page details > Unpublish). Remove it from navigation and from link web parts.
  Redirect : replace the content with a short note and a link to RedirectTo for a few months, then archive.
  Delete   : delete the page. It stays in the recycle bin for 93 days.
  Then set PageState = Retired.

Before retiring, check inbound links
  Page details and site analytics show views. A page still getting visits needs a redirect, not a delete.
  Search for the page's URL across the site to find links.

Keep retired pages out of search
  Unpublished pages are visible only to editors. For an archive that stays published, put it in a
  separate site or library excluded from search (Library settings > Advanced > Allow items to appear in search: No).

Show the date to readers
  Add the Page properties web part with PageOwner and RetireOn, labelled "Reviewed until".
stepByStepInstructions: Add owner, page type, retirement date, action and state columns to Site Pages.
Set a retirement date on every page, using defaults by page type.
Create views for pages retiring soon, past retirement and with no date.
Run a monthly flow that warns owners before the date.
Retire pages that are not extended: archive, redirect or delete, after checking inbound links.
commonMistakes: Deleting pages that other pages and bookmarks still link to.
Dates with no owner to act on them.
Extending every page automatically without reading it.
troubleshooting: If the flow finds nothing, check the columns' internal names in the filter query.
If setting properties leaves pages with unpublished changes, republish in the flow or accept a minor version for metadata.
If a retired page still appears in search, it is still published or the index has not refreshed. Unpublish and wait for the next crawl.
If owners ignore warnings, send the Past retirement view to the site manager monthly.

govern-unique-permission-exceptions.shortDescription: Set rules for when breaking permission inheritance is allowed, how it is approved and how exceptions are found and reviewed.
govern-unique-permission-exceptions.fullDescription: Unique permissions on items, folders and lists are the main reason nobody can explain who has access to what. This pattern is the policy side: when an exception is acceptable, which alternatives to try first, how to request one and how to audit them.
govern-unique-permission-exceptions.problemStatement: A site accumulates hundreds of individually shared files and folders, access reviews become impossible, and the library slows down.
whenToUse: Sites holding sensitive or mixed-audience content
Site owners who are asked to restrict or share individual items
Preparing for an access audit
whenNotToUse: Sites where everyone should see everything
Personal OneDrive content
govern-unique-permission-exceptions.formulaOrCode:
Policy in brief
  Default  : everything on a site inherits the site's permissions.
  Preferred: if a group of content needs different access, give it its own site or its own library.
  Allowed  : unique permissions on a library or a top-level folder, with an owner and a review date.
  Avoid    : unique permissions on individual files and items. Use only with approval and an expiry.

Decision guide
  Need                                              Do this
  A team's working files private from the rest      Separate site (or private channel)
  One library restricted to managers                Break inheritance on the library, use a group
  A folder shared with a supplier                   Dedicated folder with unique permissions, guest expiry set
  Each user sees only their own list items          List setting: item-level permissions (read own items)
  One confidential document                         Put it in the restricted library, do not secure the file itself
  Temporary access for a colleague                  Sharing link "Specific people" with an expiry date

Request and approval
  Request records: what, who needs access, level, reason, until when.
  Approver: the site owner. For confidential content, the information owner as well.
  Grant to a group, not individuals, wherever more than one person is involved.
  Log it (see the permissions exception log pattern) with a review date of 3 to 6 months.

Limits
  Technical: 50,000 unique permission scopes per list or library.
  Practical: performance and manageability suffer long before that. Aim for fewer than 50 per library.
  Each sharing link to specific people creates a unique scope on that item.

Find exceptions
  Site settings > Site permissions > Advanced > banner "Some content on this site has different permissions"
  > Show these items.
  PnP PowerShell:
    Get-PnPList | Where-Object { $_.HasUniqueRoleAssignments } | Select Title
    Get-PnPFolderItem -FolderSiteRelativeUrl "Shared Documents" -ItemType Folder    (then check each)
    Get-PnPListItem -List "Documents" -PageSize 2000 -Fields "FileRef","HasUniqueRoleAssignments" |
        Where-Object { $_.HasUniqueRoleAssignments } | Select @{n="Path";e={$_["FileRef"]}}
  Sharing links: Site usage > Run report.

Review (quarterly)
  For each exception: still needed? right people? could it be a folder or library instead?
  Remove: select the item > Manage access > Advanced > Delete unique permissions (restores inheritance).

Reduce the creation of exceptions
  Site sharing settings: "Only site owners can share files, folders and the site".
  Default link type: "People with existing access".
  Train owners on the decision guide above.
stepByStepInstructions: Agree the policy: inherit by default, separate sites or libraries where access differs, item-level exceptions only with approval.
Give site owners the decision guide so they choose the right structure first.
Require a logged request with a reason, an approver and a review date for each exception.
Find existing exceptions with site settings or PnP PowerShell and bring them into the log.
Review quarterly and restore inheritance where an exception is no longer needed.
commonMistakes: Securing individual files instead of placing them in a restricted library.
Granting access to named individuals who later move role.
Letting every member share, which creates unique permissions with each sharing link.
troubleshooting: If a library has become slow, count its unique scopes. Consolidate items into secured folders and restore inheritance on the items.
If a user has access nobody can explain, check sharing links on the item and its parent folders.
If restoring inheritance would remove needed access, add those people to the parent's group first.
If owners keep sharing files individually, change the site's sharing setting so only owners can share.

govern-power-apps-connected-list-changes.shortDescription: Change a SharePoint list that a Power App uses without breaking the app: what is safe, what is not and how to roll a change out.
govern-power-apps-connected-list-changes.fullDescription: A canvas app holds a cached copy of each list's schema and refers to columns by internal name. Some list changes are harmless, some need the data source refreshed, and a few break formulas. This pattern classifies them and gives a change routine.
govern-power-apps-connected-list-changes.problemStatement: A site owner deletes or retypes a column, and the app that depends on it starts failing for everyone.
whenToUse: Lists behind canvas apps or customised list forms
Lists that site owners can edit freely
Planning schema changes to a live solution
whenNotToUse: Lists with no app or flow attached
Dataverse tables, which are changed through solutions
govern-power-apps-connected-list-changes.formulaOrCode:
Effect of each list change on a canvas app

  SAFE (no app change needed)
    Add a view, change a view, column formatting
    Add a new optional column                     (the app ignores it until refreshed)
    Rename a column's DISPLAY name                (internal name is unchanged; formulas using the old display
                                                   name keep working, the new name appears after a refresh)
    Add a choice value                            (Choices() picks it up; hard-coded lists do not)

  NEEDS A REFRESH AND REPUBLISH
    New column the app should use                 Data pane > ... > Refresh, add to forms, publish
    Column changed between single and multiple selection (choice, person)
    New required column                           every Patch and form must supply it or saves fail

  BREAKS THE APP
    Delete a column the app references            formulas error; forms show a broken card
    Change a column's type                        usually not possible in place; recreating it changes the internal name
    Rename or move the list or site URL           the connection points at the old address
    Remove a choice value that formulas compare   If(Status.Value = "In review", ...) never matches
    Set "unique values" on a column with duplicates in the app's saves
    Break permissions so users lose read access to a list the app loads

Before changing a list
  1. Find what uses it: Power Apps > Apps > Details > Connections; flows that reference the list;
     the list's own Integrate > Power Apps menu for customised forms.
  2. In the app, search formulas for the column name (Search pane in Studio).
  3. Classify the change using the table above.

Rollout for a breaking change
  1. Add the NEW column alongside the old one (do not delete yet).
  2. Copy data across (grid edit or a flow).
  3. Update the app: refresh the data source, switch formulas and forms to the new column, test, publish.
  4. Update flows.
  5. After a week with no errors, hide the old column from views and forms, then delete it.
  Column deletions can be undone from the recycle bin for 93 days.

Protect the list
  Give most members Contribute (add and edit items), not Edit (which allows changing columns and views).
  Column description: "Used by the <app name> app. Contact <owner> before changing."
  Keep a short schema note: column display name, internal name, type, used by.

After any change
  Open the app in Studio > Data > Refresh the list > check the App checker for errors > Publish.
  Users get the new version when they next open the app.
stepByStepInstructions: Find the apps and flows that use the list and search the app for the column concerned.
Classify the change as safe, needing a refresh or breaking.
For breaking changes, add a new column, migrate data and update the app before removing the old one.
Refresh the data source in Studio, fix anything the App checker flags and publish.
Limit who has Edit permission on the list and document the columns the app depends on.
commonMistakes: Deleting and recreating a column to change its type, which changes the internal name.
Making a column required without updating the app's Patch calls.
Giving all members the Edit permission level, which lets them change columns.
troubleshooting: If the app shows an error on a data card after a list change, remove and re-add the card after refreshing the data source.
If Patch fails with a required field message, a column was made required. Supply it or make it optional.
If the new column does not appear in the app, refresh the data source. If it still does not, close and reopen Studio.
If a deleted column must come back, restore it from the site recycle bin so it keeps the same internal name.

govern-power-automate-service-account-ow.shortDescription: Run business-critical flows under a service account with co-owners, so they keep working when people leave or change role.
govern-power-automate-service-account-ow.fullDescription: A flow runs with the connections of whoever created them. When that person leaves, connections fail and the flow stops. This pattern covers using a dedicated service account, co-ownership, licensing and what to check when someone leaves.
govern-power-automate-service-account-ow.problemStatement: An approval flow stops silently because its owner's account was disabled, and nobody else can open it to fix the connections.
whenToUse: Flows that support business processes
Flows that send email or post on behalf of a team
Teams with staff turnover
whenNotToUse: Personal productivity flows
Flows where actions must run as the person who triggered them, which use run-only user connections
govern-power-automate-service-account-ow.formulaOrCode:
Ownership model
  Owner of connections : a service account, e.g. svc-flow-finance@contoso.com
  Co-owners            : a security group or Microsoft 365 group of two or more makers
  Run-only users       : for instant flows, the people allowed to run them

Service account setup
  [ ] A real user account (flows cannot be owned by a service principal for most connectors)
  [ ] Licence: Microsoft 365 for standard connectors; Power Automate Premium or a per-flow (Process) licence
      if the flow uses premium connectors
  [ ] Mailbox, if the flow sends email (or grant Send As on a shared mailbox and use "Send an email from a shared mailbox")
  [ ] Least privilege: site member on the sites it reads and writes, not site owner or admin
  [ ] MFA handled according to your identity team's policy for service accounts; password in a vault
  [ ] Sign-in monitored; no interactive use for day-to-day work

Build and deploy
  Prefer solutions with CONNECTION REFERENCES: makers build with their own connections in development,
  and the import into production maps each reference to the service account's connection.
  Outside solutions: sign in as the service account to create the connections, or have the service
  account be the flow's creator and add makers as co-owners.

Add co-owners
  Flow > Share > add the group as an owner. Co-owners can edit, see run history and fix connections.
  Note: each connection is still owned by whoever created it. Co-owners cannot re-authenticate
  another person's connection; they must switch the action to a connection they can use.

Inventory (one row per flow)
  FlowName | Environment | Purpose | ConnectionOwner | CoOwners | Connectors | Premium (Y/N)
  LicenceCover | BusinessOwner | FailureAlertsTo | LastReviewed

Failure alerts
  Add a catch scope in each flow that posts to a monitored channel or mailbox.
  Flow failure emails otherwise go only to the owner account. Forward the service account's mail to the team.

When someone leaves
  1. Admin: Power Platform admin center > Environments > Resources > Flows, filter by owner.
     Or PowerShell: Get-AdminFlow -EnvironmentName <env> | Where-Object { $_.CreatedBy.userId -eq <object id> }
  2. Add a new owner:  Set-AdminFlowOwnerRole -EnvironmentName <env> -FlowName <id> -PrincipalType User -RoleName CanEdit -PrincipalObjectId <new owner>
  3. Replace their connections with the service account's (edit each action, or update the connection reference).
  4. Check the flow's licence context still covers premium connectors.
  5. Run a test and confirm.

Review twice a year: flows with one owner, flows owned by disabled accounts, flows with no failure alert.
stepByStepInstructions: Create a licensed service account with only the permissions the flows need.
Build flows in solutions with connection references, and map them to the service account's connections in production.
Add a group of at least two makers as co-owners.
Send failure alerts to a monitored channel or mailbox.
Keep an inventory of flows and their connection owners, and follow a checklist when someone leaves.
commonMistakes: Assuming a co-owner can keep a flow running after the creator's account is disabled. The connections still belong to the creator.
Giving the service account admin rights.
A service account without the licence the flow's connectors need.
troubleshooting: If a flow fails with an invalid connection after someone leaves, edit the flow and switch each action to the service account's connection.
If nobody can open the flow, an admin can add an owner in the Power Platform admin center or with PowerShell.
If the flow is throttled or turned off for licensing, check the owner's licence covers premium connectors or assign a per-flow licence.
If emails come from the service account's name, send from a shared mailbox instead.

govern-sharepoint-list-naming-standards.shortDescription: Agree simple naming rules for lists, columns and views so URLs are clean, internal names are predictable and apps are easier to build.
govern-sharepoint-list-naming-standards.fullDescription: SharePoint fixes a list's URL and a column's internal name at creation. Create them with short names and no spaces, then rename the display name, and every formula, flow and REST call becomes simpler. This pattern sets out the rules.
govern-sharepoint-list-naming-standards.problemStatement: Flows and apps are full of names like Request_x0020_Due_x0020_Date and field_7, because lists and columns were created with spaces or imported from Excel.
whenToUse: Any list that an app, flow or integration will use
Teams with more than one maker
Before building, since internal names cannot be changed later
whenNotToUse: Throwaway lists
Existing lists in use, where recreating columns would break things
govern-sharepoint-list-naming-standards.formulaOrCode:
Why it matters
  A list's URL and a column's internal name are set when they are created and never change.
  Spaces become _x0020_, special characters become other codes, and long names are cut at 32 characters.
  "Request Due Date"  ->  internal name  Request_x0020_Due_x0020_Date
  Flows, REST filters, JSON formatting and some Power Fx all use the internal name.

The create-then-rename technique
  1. Create the list as   ITRequests        (URL: /Lists/ITRequests)
     then rename it to     IT Requests       (display name; URL stays clean)
  2. Create the column as  DueDate
     then rename it to     Due date
  Result: friendly names for users, tidy names for makers.

List names
  Create: PascalCase, no spaces, plural noun, optional short prefix for the solution
          ITRequests, FacilitiesRequests, RefDepartments, LogStatusHistory
  Prefixes that help: Ref (reference data), Log (history or audit), Cfg (settings)
  Display: plain words, "IT Requests"
  Avoid : dates or versions in names (Requests2025, Requests_v2), "New", "Test" on anything that goes live

Column names
  Create: PascalCase, no spaces, under 32 characters, describe the value
          DueDate, AssignedTo, ApprovalStatus, IsUrgent, CostCentre
  Yes/No     : start with Is or Has        IsActive, HasAttachments
  Dates      : end with Date or On         ReviewDate, ClosedOn
  People     : role, not "Person"          Approver, Requester
  Lookups    : the thing referred to       Project, Department
  Do not reuse built-in names: Title, ID, Created, Modified, Author, Editor, Name.
  Avoid : starting with a digit, symbols such as % # & /, and reserved words

  Title column: keep it, rename the display name to something meaningful ("Request summary").
  Internal name remains Title.

Views
  Name by audience and filter: "My open requests", "Overdue", "Awaiting approval"
  Create with no spaces if you will link to the view's URL (MyOpen.aspx), then rename.

Lists created from Excel or CSV
  Columns get internal names field_1, field_2 ... Avoid for anything long-lived.
  Create the list and columns by hand or from a template, then paste data in grid view.

Find internal names
  Column settings page: the URL ends with Field=<InternalName>
  Or: _api/web/lists/getbytitle('IT Requests')/fields?$select=Title,InternalName&$filter=Hidden eq false

Record the standard
  One page: the rules above, the prefixes in use, and a table of each solution's lists.
  Review new lists before go-live. Renaming later fixes only the display name.
stepByStepInstructions: Agree the rules for list, column and view names and write them on one page.
Create each list and column with a short PascalCase name and no spaces.
Rename the display name to friendly text straight afterwards.
Avoid creating long-lived lists from Excel imports.
Check internal names before go-live, since they cannot be changed later.
commonMistakes: Creating a column with its friendly name, spaces included.
Importing from Excel and living with field_1, field_2.
Putting years or versions in list names.
troubleshooting: If an internal name is already awkward and the list is in use, leave it and document it. Recreating the column breaks apps and flows.
If a flow cannot find a column, use its internal name, which you can read from the column settings URL.
If two columns appear to share a name, one is a renamed column whose internal name differs.
If a name is cut off, internal names are limited to 32 characters, and encoded spaces count as seven each.

govern-launch-communications-for-site-ch.shortDescription: Plan what to tell people, when and how, before changing a SharePoint site they rely on.
govern-launch-communications-for-site-ch.fullDescription: Moving a library, changing navigation or replacing a list with an app breaks habits and bookmarks. A short communications plan, matched to the size of the change, prevents most of the confusion and support requests.
govern-launch-communications-for-site-ch.problemStatement: A site is reorganised over a weekend, and on Monday people cannot find their documents and assume they have been deleted.
whenToUse: Navigation, structure or permission changes on a used site
Replacing a list or form with a Power App
Migrations and site retirements
whenNotToUse: Changes users will not notice
New sites with no existing audience
govern-launch-communications-for-site-ch.formulaOrCode:
1. Size the change
   Small  : a new view, a renamed column, an extra page                  -> note in the team channel on the day
   Medium : navigation changes, a library reorganised, a new form or app -> plan below, one week's notice
   Large  : site migration, permission model change, site retirement     -> plan below, 3 to 4 weeks' notice, sponsor message

2. Know the audience
   Who uses the site: Site usage > unique viewers; the site's members group; teams that link to it.
   Segment: everyday users | occasional users | owners and editors | people with links or synced libraries.

3. Plan (medium and large changes)
   When            What                                                Channel                      Owner
   T-3 weeks       What is changing, why, and when (large only)        Email from sponsor + news     Sponsor
   T-1 week        What you need to do; what will look different       Email + Teams post            Site owner
   T-1 week        Banner on the site's home page with the date        Text web part                 Site owner
   T-1 day         Reminder with the exact time and any downtime       Teams post                    Site owner
   Day 0           "It's live": where things are now, with links       Email + Teams + banner update Site owner
   Day 0 to +5     Help available: drop-in, channel, contact           Teams channel                 Support lead
   T+2 weeks       What we fixed from feedback; remove banner          Teams post                    Site owner

4. Every message answers
   What is changing?            One sentence, no jargon.
   When?                        Date and time, with time zone.
   What do I need to do?        Usually: update bookmarks, re-sync, use the new link. Say "nothing" if nothing.
   What will be different?      One before-and-after screenshot.
   Where do I get help?         A channel or mailbox, not a person.

5. Technical steps that save support calls
   Old locations : leave a "This has moved" page or a link in the old library for at least 30 days.
   Moved files   : Move to (not download and upload) keeps version history and redirects many old links.
   Renamed site  : SharePoint redirects the old URL; test it. Flows and apps may still need updating.
   Synced folders: tell users to stop syncing the old library and sync the new one.
   Bookmarks, Teams tabs, navigation links, email signatures: list them and update what you control.
   Permissions   : compare before and after for one user per group.

6. Track it
   A list: Message | Audience | Channel | Owner | PlannedDate | SentDate | Status
   And a feedback log for the first two weeks: issue, who raised it, fix, date.

7. Check it landed
   Day +1: are the new pages getting visits? Are support questions about finding things? Adjust the banner and FAQ.
stepByStepInstructions: Size the change as small, medium or large and choose the notice period.
Identify who uses the site and how, including people with synced libraries and bookmarks.
Schedule messages before, on and after the change date, each with an owner and channel.
Make every message say what changes, when, what to do and where to get help.
Leave signposts at old locations, offer help for the first week and act on feedback.
commonMistakes: Announcing once, on the day.
Explaining the reasons at length and burying what users need to do.
Deleting the old location with no pointer to the new one.
troubleshooting: If people say they were not told, use more than one channel and put a banner on the site itself.
If old links are broken, check whether files were moved or copied. Moves redirect in many cases, copies do not.
If synced libraries show errors, users are still syncing the old location. Send the re-sync steps.
If support requests cluster on one topic, add it to the home page banner and the FAQ the same day.

create-a-dataverse-table-naming-standard.shortDescription: Agree how tables, columns, relationships and keys are named in Dataverse before the first table is created, because schema names cannot be changed afterwards.
create-a-dataverse-table-naming-standard.fullDescription: Dataverse gives every table and column two names: a display name you can change at any time and a schema name that is fixed at creation. A short naming standard, applied from the first table, keeps formulas, flows, FetchXML and Web API calls readable for the life of the solution.
create-a-dataverse-table-naming-standard.problemStatement: Tables created without a standard end up with names like cr3a1_newtable2 and columns such as new_field1, and nothing can be renamed once apps and flows depend on them.
whenToUse: Before creating the first table in a new solution
When several makers build in the same environment
When apps will be moved between environments as managed solutions
whenNotToUse: Throwaway prototypes in a personal developer environment
Tables owned by another publisher, which keep their own prefix
create-a-dataverse-table-naming-standard.formulaOrCode:
Publisher
  Create one publisher per organisation or product line, before any table.
  Prefix: 3 to 8 lowercase letters, for example  contoso  ->  contoso_
  Never build in the Default publisher (prefix such as cr3a1_ or new_).

Tables
  Display name   singular, title case           Service Request
  Plural name    plural                          Service Requests
  Schema name    prefix + PascalCase singular    contoso_ServiceRequest
  Logical name   lowercase, set automatically    contoso_servicerequest
  Entity set     used by the Web API             contoso_servicerequests

Columns
  Type            Display name        Schema name
  Text            Request Title       contoso_RequestTitle        (or use the primary name column)
  Choice          Priority            contoso_Priority
  Yes/No          Is Urgent           contoso_IsUrgent            starts with Is or Has
  Date only       Needed By           contoso_NeededByDate        ends with Date
  Date and time   Submitted On        contoso_SubmittedOn         ends with On
  Lookup          Requester           contoso_RequesterId         ends with Id
  Currency        Estimated Cost      contoso_EstimatedCost
  Whole number    Item Count          contoso_ItemCount

Primary name column
  Keep it meaningful: Request Number or Title, not the default "Name".

Relationships
  Parent_Child, using table schema names:   contoso_Project_ServiceRequest
  Many-to-many intersect table:             contoso_ServiceRequest_Tag

Global choices
  contoso_RequestStatus, contoso_Priority    reuse them across tables instead of local copies.

Alternate keys
  contoso_RequestNumberKey

Where each name appears
  Power Fx            display names:   'Service Requests', 'Needed By'
  Power Automate      logical names in filters:   contoso_neededbydate ge 2026-11-01
                      lookups in filters:         _contoso_requesterid_value eq <guid>
  Web API             entity set name:  /api/data/v9.2/contoso_servicerequests
  FetchXML            logical names

Before saving a new table or column
  Open Advanced options and check the schema name. The maker portal builds it from the first
  display name you type, including typing mistakes.
stepByStepInstructions: Create a solution publisher with a short, meaningful prefix.
Create a solution that uses that publisher and build every table inside it.
Write the naming rules for tables, columns, relationships and choices on one page.
Check the schema name under Advanced options every time before saving a new table or column.
Use global choices for values shared by more than one table.
Review new tables against the standard before they are exported to test.
commonMistakes: Building in the Default solution, so components get a random prefix.
Accepting the schema name generated from a mistyped display name.
Using plural names for tables, which produces awkward entity set names.
Creating a local choice on each table for the same list of values.
troubleshooting: If a column has the wrong schema name, delete and recreate it before any data or app depends on it. Schema names cannot be edited.
If a flow filter fails on a lookup column, use the form _prefix_columnname_value with the row's GUID.
If two environments show different prefixes for the same table, it was created outside the solution in one of them. Rebuild it under the correct publisher.
If Power Fx shows a different name from the flow, Power Fx uses display names while flows and the Web API use logical names.

faqs.question: Can I rename a Dataverse table or column later?
faqs.answer: You can change the display name at any time. The schema and logical names are fixed when the table or column is created.

faqs.question: What prefix should a Dataverse table have?
faqs.answer: The prefix of your own solution publisher, such as contoso_. Avoid the default publisher's prefix, which is random and tells nobody who owns the component.

faqs.question: Should Dataverse table names be singular or plural?
faqs.answer: Singular for the display and schema name. Dataverse asks for a separate plural name and builds the Web API entity set name from it.

create-a-request-table-schema.shortDescription: A Dataverse table design for a request or ticket app: columns, choices, relationships, keys and views that work with model-driven and canvas apps.
create-a-request-table-schema.fullDescription: Most business apps start with a request: someone asks for something, somebody else reviews it, and it ends approved, rejected or completed. This schema gives that table the columns and relationships it needs in Dataverse, using built-in features such as status reason, ownership and autonumber instead of rebuilding them.
create-a-request-table-schema.problemStatement: Request tables copied from a spreadsheet miss ownership, status history and keys, so security, reporting and integration all need rework later.
whenToUse: Building a request, ticket, intake or case-style app on Dataverse
Moving a SharePoint request list to Dataverse
Apps that need row-level security by owner or team
whenNotToUse: Customer service scenarios already covered by Dynamics 365 Case
Simple lists with a few hundred rows and no security needs, where a SharePoint list is enough
create-a-request-table-schema.formulaOrCode:
Table: Service Request (contoso_ServiceRequest)
  Ownership : User or team          (gives row-level security by owner and business unit)
  Options   : Track changes on, Auditing on, Attachments if files are needed

Columns
  Display name        Type                      Notes
  Request Number      Autonumber (primary name) format REQ-{SEQNUM:6}
  Title               Text (200)                required
  Description         Multiline text
  Category            Lookup -> Request Category   reference table, so the business can maintain it
  Priority            Choice (global)           Low | Medium | High     default Medium
  Requester           Lookup -> User            defaults to the creator in the app
  Requester Department Text or Lookup           snapshot at submission
  Needed By           Date only
  Submitted On        Date and time
  Assigned To         use the built-in Owner column, or a second Lookup -> User
  Decision            Choice                    Approved | Rejected | Deferred
  Decision By         Lookup -> User
  Decision On         Date and time
  Decision Comments   Multiline text
  Estimated Cost      Currency

Status (built in)
  Status          Status reason
  Active          Draft | Submitted | In review | Waiting for requester
  Inactive        Completed | Rejected | Cancelled
  Use Status reason for the lifecycle. Do not add a second custom status column.

Related tables
  Request Category  (Name, Is Active, Default Assignee)                 1:N to Service Request
  Request Task      (Name, Due Date, Is Complete, lookup to request)    N:1, delete behaviour Cascade
  Notes / Timeline  enable for comments and attachments

Alternate key
  Request Number   lets integrations upsert by number instead of GUID.

Views
  My Active Requests        Requester equals current user, Status = Active
  Awaiting Review           Status reason = Submitted, sorted by Submitted On
  My Team's Open Requests   Owner equals current user's teams
  Closed This Month         Status = Inactive, Modified On this month

Canvas app formulas
  Filter('Service Requests', Requester.'Primary Email' = User().Email && Status = 'Status (Service Requests)'.Active)
  Patch('Service Requests', Defaults('Service Requests'), {
      Title: txtTitle.Value,
      Priority: 'Priority'.High,
      Category: ddCategory.Selected,
      'Status Reason': 'Status Reason (Service Requests)'.Submitted
  })
stepByStepInstructions: Create the table in a solution with user or team ownership.
Set the primary name column to an autonumber request number.
Add the columns, using lookups for people and categories and global choices for shared values.
Edit the Status reason values to match the request lifecycle.
Create the category and task tables and their relationships.
Add an alternate key on the request number.
Create the views, then build the model-driven form or canvas screens.
commonMistakes: Choosing organization ownership, which removes row-level security and cannot be changed later.
Adding a custom status choice instead of using Status and Status reason.
Storing people as text email addresses instead of lookups to User.
Leaving the primary name column as a free-text Name that users must invent.
troubleshooting: If users cannot see each other's requests, check the security role's read access level on the table (User, Business Unit or Organization).
If a canvas filter on status shows a delegation warning, compare with the choice enum value, not with text.
If the autonumber did not fill on existing rows, it applies only to rows created after the column was added.
If deleting a request leaves orphaned tasks, set the relationship's delete behaviour to Cascade.

faqs.question: Should a Dataverse request table be user-owned or organization-owned?
faqs.answer: User or team owned. That gives each row an owner and lets security roles limit access by user, business unit or organisation. The choice cannot be changed after the table is created.

faqs.question: How do I create a request number in Dataverse?
faqs.answer: Use an autonumber column, ideally as the primary name column, with a format such as REQ-{SEQNUM:6}.

faqs.question: Should I use Status reason or my own choice column?
faqs.answer: Use the built-in Status and Status reason. Views, deactivation, business process flows and reporting all understand them.

create-a-lookup-relationship-model.shortDescription: Plan Dataverse relationships before building: which tables are parents, which behaviours apply on delete and reassign, and when a many-to-many is the right choice.
create-a-lookup-relationship-model.fullDescription: Relationships decide what users see on forms, what happens when a parent row is deleted or reassigned, and how security flows from parent to child. A short relationship model, drawn before tables are created, prevents the two most expensive mistakes: the wrong direction and the wrong cascade behaviour.
create-a-lookup-relationship-model.problemStatement: Lookups get added one at a time as screens need them, leaving circular references, orphaned rows and child records that the right people cannot see.
whenToUse: Designing a solution with more than two or three tables
When child rows must follow their parent's owner or sharing
When deciding between a lookup, a many-to-many or a choice
whenNotToUse: A single table with no related data
Short fixed lists with no attributes, where a choice column is simpler
create-a-lookup-relationship-model.formulaOrCode:
Relationship register (one row per relationship)
  Parent (one)       Child (many)        Lookup on child     Type           Delete parent    Required
  Project            Service Request     Project             Referential    Remove link      No
  Service Request    Request Task        Service Request     Parental       Cascade          Yes
  Request Category   Service Request     Category            Referential    Restrict         Yes
  Service Request    Tag                 (intersect table)   Many-to-many   n/a              n/a

Relationship behaviour types
  Parental                 child follows parent for assign, share, reparent and delete (all Cascade)
  Referential              rows are linked only; deleting the parent clears the lookup
  Referential, Restrict    parent cannot be deleted while children exist
  Custom                   choose each action yourself

Cascade options per action (Custom)
  Assign / Share / Unshare / Reparent : Cascade All | Cascade Active | Cascade User-owned | Cascade None
  Delete                              : Cascade All | Remove Link | Restrict
  A table can have only ONE parental (cascading) relationship.

Choosing the type
  Child has no meaning without the parent (task, line item)        -> Parental
  Child refers to reference data (category, department)            -> Referential, Restrict delete
  Either side can exist alone, link is optional                    -> Referential, Remove link
  Many on both sides, no data about the link itself                -> Many-to-many (native)
  Many on both sides, link has its own data (role, dates)          -> Manual intersect table with two lookups

Special lookups
  Customer   points to Account or Contact
  Owner      points to User or Team
  Regarding  (activities) points to many table types
  Polymorphic lookup: one column, several target tables, created through the API or XrmToolBox.

Using lookups
  Power Fx     Filter('Request Tasks', 'Service Request'.'Service Request' = selectedRequest.'Service Request')
               Patch('Request Tasks', Defaults('Request Tasks'), { Name: "Review", 'Service Request': selectedRequest })
               selectedTask.'Service Request'.Title            (walk up to the parent)
               selectedRequest.'Request Tasks'                 (walk down to children)
  Power Automate (Add a new row)   Service Request:  contoso_servicerequests(<guid>)
  Flow filter                      _contoso_servicerequestid_value eq <guid>
stepByStepInstructions: List the tables and draw a line for each relationship, marking the one and many sides.
For each line, decide whether the child can exist without the parent.
Pick the behaviour type and write it in the register.
Check that no table has more than one parental relationship.
Decide which lookups are required.
Create the relationships in the solution and test delete and reassign with sample rows.
commonMistakes: Leaving every relationship on the default Referential when child rows should be deleted with the parent.
Trying to make two parental relationships on one table.
Using a native many-to-many when the link needs its own columns, such as a role or start date.
Creating the lookup on the wrong table, so the one and many sides are reversed.
troubleshooting: If a parent row cannot be deleted, a Restrict relationship has child rows. Delete or move the children first.
If child rows did not change owner with the parent, the relationship's Assign behaviour is not set to Cascade.
If Dataverse refuses a parental relationship, the child table already has one. Use Referential for the second.
If a flow fails setting a lookup, pass the entity set name and GUID in the form contoso_servicerequests(guid).

faqs.question: What is the difference between parental and referential relationships in Dataverse?
faqs.answer: In a parental relationship, actions on the parent such as delete, assign and share cascade to the children. In a referential relationship the rows are only linked, and the children are unaffected.

faqs.question: Can a Dataverse table have two parents?
faqs.answer: It can have many lookups, but only one relationship can be parental. Others must be referential.

faqs.question: When should I use a many-to-many relationship?
faqs.answer: When rows on both sides can link to many on the other and you do not need to store anything about the link. If the link needs its own data, create an intersect table with two lookups.

create-a-choice-column-strategy.shortDescription: Decide when to use a choice, a multi-select choice, a Yes/No column or a lookup table in Dataverse, and how to manage choice values across environments.
create-a-choice-column-strategy.fullDescription: Choices in Dataverse are stored as numbers with labels, live in solutions, and can be global or local. Lookups are stored as references to rows that business users can maintain. Picking the right one for each list of values avoids deployments for simple data changes and keeps filtering fast.
create-a-choice-column-strategy.problemStatement: Lists that change weekly are built as choices and need a solution deployment for each new value, while fixed lists are built as tables that nobody maintains.
whenToUse: Designing columns that hold a value from a list
Standardising choices used on more than one table
Planning how list values move from development to production
whenNotToUse: Free-text fields
Status lifecycle, which belongs in the built-in Status reason column
create-a-choice-column-strategy.formulaOrCode:
Decision table
  Question                                              Choice     Lookup table
  Who changes the values?                               a maker    business users, in the app
  How often do they change?                             rarely     often
  Does each value need extra data (owner, active, order)?  no      yes
  Do values differ per environment?                     no         can do
  Is it used to drive logic in formulas and flows?      good       needs care (compare by key, not name)
  Number of values                                      under ~30  any
  Needs filtering by another column (cascading)?        hard       natural

Global or local choice
  Global   one definition reused by several tables.   contoso_Priority
  Local    belongs to one column.                      Only when the list is truly unique to it.
  Prefer global. A local choice cannot be converted to global later.

Values
  Each option has a label and a number. The number starts with the publisher's option value prefix,
  for example 100000000, 100000001.
  Never reuse a number for a new meaning. Retire an option by renaming it "(Retired) X" or
  removing it once no row uses it.
  Set colours on options. Model-driven views and charts use them.

Multi-select choice (Choices)
  Fine for tagging. Cannot be used in rollups, calculated columns, or sorted, and filtering is limited.
  If you need to report on each value, use a many-to-many to a reference table.

Yes/No
  Two fixed options with labels you can rename (for example Approved / Not approved).
  If a third state may ever appear, use a choice from the start.

Power Fx
  Read label           Text(ThisItem.Priority)
  Compare              ThisItem.Priority = 'Priority'.High
  Filter (delegable)   Filter('Service Requests', Priority = 'Priority'.High)
  Dropdown items       Choices('Priority')
  Patch                Patch('Service Requests', selectedRequest, { Priority: 'Priority'.Low })
  Multi-select         Patch(..., { Tags: [ 'Tags'.Urgent, 'Tags'.External ] })

Power Automate
  Filter rows          contoso_priority eq 100000002
  Label in outputs     contoso_priority@OData.Community.Display.V1.FormattedValue
  expression           outputs('Get_a_row_by_ID')?['body/contoso_priority@OData.Community.Display.V1.FormattedValue']

Deployment
  Choices travel in the solution. Adding a value in production directly creates an unmanaged
  layer that hides later updates. Add values in development and deploy.
stepByStepInstructions: List every column that holds a value from a list.
Apply the decision table and mark each as choice, Yes/No or lookup.
Create global choices for lists used by more than one table.
Create reference tables with an active flag and sort order for business-maintained lists.
Set colours and default values on choices.
Document the option numbers used in flows and integrations.
commonMistakes: Using a choice for a list the business changes every month.
Comparing choice labels as text in flows instead of the option number.
Creating the same local choice on several tables.
Adding choice values directly in production.
troubleshooting: If a flow condition never matches, it compares the label. Use the numeric value or the FormattedValue property.
If a new value is missing after deployment, an unmanaged layer in the target environment is overriding the choice. Remove the active layer.
If a canvas app shows a number instead of text, wrap the value in Text().
If a multi-select choice cannot be used in a view filter the way you need, move the values to a related table.

faqs.question: Should I use a choice or a lookup in Dataverse?
faqs.answer: Use a choice for short, stable lists that makers control. Use a lookup to a reference table when business users maintain the values, when values need extra attributes, or when they change often.

faqs.question: What is the difference between a global and a local choice?
faqs.answer: A global choice is defined once and reused by many columns. A local choice belongs to a single column and cannot be shared or converted later.

faqs.question: How do I filter by a choice column in Power Automate?
faqs.answer: Use the option's numeric value in the filter, such as contoso_priority eq 100000002. The label is available in the outputs as the FormattedValue property.

create-a-business-rule-checklist.shortDescription: A checklist for deciding where logic belongs in Dataverse (business rule, calculated or formula column, real-time flow, plug-in or app formula) and for building business rules that behave predictably.
create-a-business-rule-checklist.fullDescription: Business rules are the quickest way to add validation and field behaviour to a Dataverse table without code, and they can run on the server so every app and import respects them. They also have firm limits. This checklist keeps each rule small, scoped correctly and documented.
create-a-business-rule-checklist.problemStatement: Validation is rebuilt in every app and flow, or packed into one giant business rule that nobody can follow and that silently fails to run from a canvas app.
whenToUse: Adding required-if, show/hide, default value or simple validation logic to a table
When the same rule must apply in model-driven apps, canvas apps and imports
Reviewing an inherited solution's rules
whenNotToUse: Logic that reads or writes related rows, which needs a flow, plug-in or low-code plug-in
Complex calculations better held in a formula or calculated column
create-a-business-rule-checklist.formulaOrCode:
Where should the logic live?
  Need                                                   Use
  Require a field when another has a value               Business rule
  Show, hide, lock or unlock a field on a form           Business rule (scope: form or All Forms)
  Set a default or copy a value on the same row          Business rule
  Show an error and block save                           Business rule (scope: Entity to enforce on the server)
  Value derived from the same row or its parent          Formula column (Power Fx) or calculated column
  Aggregate child rows (count, sum)                      Rollup column
  Create or update other rows                            Real-time workflow, low-code plug-in, or cloud flow
  Call an external system                                Cloud flow or plug-in
  Screen behaviour in one canvas app only                Power Fx in the app

Scope
  Entity (Table)   runs on the server for every create and update, and on all model-driven forms.
                   Canvas apps and flows get the result when the row is saved.
  All Forms        client side, all main forms and quick create. Not enforced for canvas, flows or imports.
  <Form name>      one form only.

What a business rule can do
  Set field value | Clear field value | Set business required | Set visibility (forms only)
  Lock or unlock (forms only) | Show error message | Recommendation (forms only)
  Conditions use fields on the same table only. Up to ten if-else conditions in one rule.

Checklist for each rule
  [ ] Name states the outcome:  Require Decision Comments when Rejected
  [ ] Description says why and who asked for it
  [ ] Scope is Entity if it must hold outside model-driven forms
  [ ] Has an else branch that reverses the action (unlock, show, not required)
  [ ] Uses only actions that are supported at its scope
  [ ] Error message tells the user what to enter
  [ ] Tested on create, update, quick create, import and from the canvas app
  [ ] Activated, and in the solution

Example
  Rule  : Require Decision Comments when Rejected       Scope: Entity
  IF      Decision equals Rejected
  THEN    Set Decision Comments as Business Required
  ELSE    Set Decision Comments as Not Business Required

  Rule  : Needed By cannot be in the past               Scope: Entity
  IF      Needed By is less than Created On
  THEN    Show error message on Needed By: "Choose a date after today."

Canvas apps
  Entity-scope rules that set values or show errors are applied on save; the error comes back
  through the form's OnFailure or IfError. Visibility and lock actions do not carry over, so
  repeat those in the app's formulas.
stepByStepInstructions: Write each requirement as one sentence and place it using the table above.
Create the business rule from the table's Business rules tab inside the solution.
Set the scope before adding conditions.
Add the condition, the action and a reversing else branch.
Validate, save and activate the rule.
Test it from every entry point, including the canvas app and an import.
commonMistakes: Leaving scope on a single form and expecting the rule to apply in a canvas app.
No else branch, so a field stays locked or required after the condition stops being true.
Several rules setting the same field, with the result depending on run order.
Using a business rule where a formula column would do the job with less upkeep.
troubleshooting: If a rule does not run in a canvas app, set its scope to Entity. Only server-side actions apply there.
If a rule does nothing on a form, a field it references is not on that form. Add the field, hidden if needed.
If a field stays required after the condition clears, add the else branch that sets it back.
If the rule will not activate, it uses an action that is not supported at Entity scope, such as visibility.

faqs.question: Do Dataverse business rules work in canvas apps?
faqs.answer: Rules with Entity scope run on the server when a row is saved, so set-value, required and error actions apply. Show, hide and lock actions only work on model-driven forms.

faqs.question: What is the difference between a business rule and a formula column?
faqs.answer: A business rule applies actions such as required, default and error messages. A formula column stores a calculation that is always up to date and can be used in views and filters.

faqs.question: How many conditions can a business rule have?
