faqs.answer: Up to ten if-else conditions in one rule. Split larger logic into several small rules with clear names.

create-a-security-role-matrix.shortDescription: Lay out who can create, read, write, delete, append, assign and share each Dataverse table, at which access level, before building security roles.
create-a-security-role-matrix.fullDescription: A security role is a grid of tables against privileges, each set to an access level. Building roles directly in the editor makes it hard to see the whole picture. A matrix agreed with the business first turns role creation into a transcription job and becomes the test script afterwards.
create-a-security-role-matrix.problemStatement: Roles are copied from System Customizer or Basic User and adjusted until the app stops showing errors, leaving users with far more access than anyone intended.
whenToUse: Any Dataverse app with more than one type of user
Before go-live security testing
Reviewing access after an audit finding
whenNotToUse: Personal productivity apps in a developer environment
Dataverse for Teams, which uses fixed Owner, Member and Guest roles
create-a-security-role-matrix.formulaOrCode:
Access levels
  None | User (own rows) | Business Unit | Parent: Child Business Units | Organization
  Organization-owned tables only offer None or Organization.

Privileges
  Create | Read | Write | Delete | Append | Append To | Assign | Share

Matrix (example)
  Table              Requester            Reviewer                 Manager               Admin
  Service Request    C:User  R:User       C:None R:BU              R:BU   W:BU           all: Org
                     W:User  D:None       W:BU   D:None            D:None Assign:BU
                     Append:User          Append/AppendTo:BU       Share:BU
                     AppendTo:User        Assign:BU
  Request Task       C/R/W:User           C/R/W:BU                 R:BU                  all: Org
  Request Category   R:Org                R:Org                    R:Org                 C/R/W/D:Org
  Note (Timeline)    C/R:User AppendTo    C/R/W:BU                 R:BU                  all: Org
  Activity           R:User               C/R/W:BU                 R:BU                  all: Org

Append and Append To
  To attach a Task to a Request the user needs Append on Task and Append To on Request.
  Setting a lookup counts as appending. Missing one of the pair is the most common cause of
  "you do not have permission" on save.

Build the roles
  1. Copy the "App Opener" role (minimum privileges to run an app) or "Basic User".
     Do not start from System Customizer.
  2. Name:  Contoso Requests - Requester
  3. Set table privileges from the matrix.
  4. Add the roles to the solution.
  5. Roles are cumulative: a user gets the highest access any of their roles grants.

Assign through teams
  Create a Microsoft Entra ID security group per role.
  Create a Dataverse team of type "Microsoft Entra ID Security Group" linked to it.
  Assign the security role to the team. Membership is then managed in Entra ID.
  For user-owned rows, set the role's "Member's privilege inheritance" to
  Direct User (Basic) access level and Team privileges.

Beyond roles
  Row sharing              one-off access to a single row
  Access teams             many users on specific rows without a role per row
  Column security profile  hide or lock sensitive columns such as salary
  Business units           separate data by division; consider only when divisions must not see each other

Test script (one line per cell)
  As Requester: create a request (pass), open a colleague's request (fail), delete own request (fail).
stepByStepInstructions: List user types and the tables in the solution.
Fill in the matrix with the business owner, one cell at a time.
Copy App Opener or Basic User and set privileges from the matrix.
Create Entra ID groups and group teams, and assign roles to the teams.
Share the app with the same groups.
Run the test script with a test account for each role.
commonMistakes: Copying System Customizer or System Administrator as the starting point.
Granting Organization-level read because Business Unit looked complicated.
Forgetting Append and Append To for lookups.
Assigning roles to individual users instead of group teams.
troubleshooting: If a user gets a permission error on save, read the error's privilege name, such as prvAppendTocontoso_servicerequest, and add that privilege.
If a user sees no rows, their read access level is User and the rows are owned by someone else.
If a role assigned to a team has no effect on user-owned rows, set the role's member privilege inheritance to include direct user access.
If the app will not open, the user lacks the basic privileges in App Opener or Basic User.

faqs.question: What are the access levels in a Dataverse security role?
faqs.answer: None, User, Business Unit, Parent: Child Business Units and Organization. They control which rows a privilege applies to, from the user's own rows up to every row.

faqs.question: What is the difference between Append and Append To?
faqs.answer: Append lets you attach the row to another row. Append To lets other rows be attached to it. Linking a child to a parent needs Append on the child and Append To on the parent.

faqs.question: Should I assign security roles to users or teams?
faqs.answer: To teams linked to Entra ID security groups. Access is then managed by group membership and is easier to audit.

create-an-environment-variable-register.shortDescription: Keep one list of every environment variable in a solution, with its type, purpose and value per environment, so deployments never go out with a development URL.
create-an-environment-variable-register.fullDescription: Environment variables hold the settings that differ between development, test and production: site URLs, list IDs, email addresses, feature switches and secrets. A register records what each one is for and what value it should have in each environment, and doubles as the source for the deployment settings file.
create-an-environment-variable-register.problemStatement: After import, a production flow writes to the development SharePoint site because nobody knew which variables existed or what their production values should be.
whenToUse: Any solution deployed to more than one environment
Before the first managed import to test
When handing a solution to a support team
whenNotToUse: Unmanaged personal apps that never leave one environment
Values users should change in the app, which belong in a settings table
create-an-environment-variable-register.formulaOrCode:
Register
  Display name            Schema name                 Type          Dev value                 Test value                Prod value                Used by
  SharePoint Site         contoso_SharePointSite      Data source   .../sites/Requests-Dev    .../sites/Requests-Test   .../sites/Requests        Request app, Approval flow
  Requests List           contoso_RequestsList        Data source   Requests (in the site)    Requests                  Requests                  Request app, Approval flow
  Support Mailbox         contoso_SupportMailbox      Text          dev-support@contoso.com   test-support@...          support@contoso.com       Error handler flow
  Approval Timeout Days   contoso_ApprovalTimeoutDays Decimal       1                         1                         5                         Approval flow
  Enable Teams Alerts     contoso_EnableTeamsAlerts   Yes/No        No                        Yes                       Yes                       Notification flow
  API Key                 contoso_ApiKey              Secret        Key Vault reference per environment                                           Integration flow
  Routing Rules           contoso_RoutingRules        JSON          { "default": "..." }                                                          Approval flow

Types
  Text | Decimal number | Yes/No | JSON | Data source (SharePoint site and list, Dataverse, SAP, SQL) | Secret (Azure Key Vault)

Default value and current value
  Default value   travels with the solution.
  Current value   belongs to the environment.
  Before exporting, remove the current value from the solution (variable > ... > Remove from this
  solution) so the development value is not shipped. The importer is then prompted for a value.

Deployment settings file (pac CLI), built from the register
  pac solution create-settings --solution-zip Requests_managed.zip --settings-file settings.prod.json
  {
    "EnvironmentVariables": [
      { "SchemaName": "contoso_SupportMailbox", "Value": "support@contoso.com" },
      { "SchemaName": "contoso_ApprovalTimeoutDays", "Value": "5" }
    ],
    "ConnectionReferences": [
      { "LogicalName": "contoso_SharePointRequests", "ConnectionId": "<connection id>", "ConnectorId": "/providers/Microsoft.PowerApps/apis/shared_sharepointonline" }
    ]
  }
  pac solution import --path Requests_managed.zip --settings-file settings.prod.json

Read a variable
  Power Automate   Dynamic content > Environment variables, or  parameters('Support Mailbox (contoso_SupportMailbox)')
  Canvas app       add the tables Environment Variable Definitions and Environment Variable Values, then
                   LookUp('Environment Variable Values',
                          'Environment Variable Definition'.'Schema Name' = "contoso_SupportMailbox").Value
                   Data source variables are used by picking them when adding the SharePoint connection.

List all variables and current values (Web API)
  GET /api/data/v9.2/environmentvariabledefinitions?$select=schemaname,displayname,defaultvalue,type
      &$expand=environmentvariabledefinition_environmentvariablevalue($select=value)
stepByStepInstructions: Open the solution and filter to Environment variables.
Add each one to the register with its type and purpose.
Agree the value for each environment with the owner of that system.
Remove current values from the solution before export.
Generate a settings file per environment from the register.
After each import, compare the environment's current values with the register.
commonMistakes: Exporting with current values included, so development settings overwrite the target.
Storing secrets as text variables instead of Key Vault references.
Hard-coding a URL in one flow action while a variable exists for it.
Creating variables outside the solution, so they do not travel with it.
troubleshooting: If a flow still uses the old value after a change, turn the flow off and on. Flows cache environment variable values.
If a canvas app shows the old data source, it reads data source variables at publish time in some cases. Republish after changing the value.
If import does not ask for values, the solution already contains current values. Remove them in development and export again.
If a secret variable fails, the environment's Dataverse service principal needs the Key Vault Secrets User role on the vault.

faqs.question: What is the difference between the default value and the current value of an environment variable?
faqs.answer: The default value is part of the solution and moves with it. The current value is set in each environment and overrides the default there.

faqs.question: How do I set environment variable values during deployment?
faqs.answer: Remove current values before export, then supply values at import, either in the import dialog, a deployment settings file with the pac CLI, or the pipeline's deployment settings.

faqs.question: Can canvas apps read environment variables?
faqs.answer: Yes. Data source variables are used directly when adding a connection. Other values are read from the Environment Variable Values table with LookUp.

create-a-solution-aware-data-model.shortDescription: Build Dataverse tables inside a solution from the first day so the data model, apps and flows can be deployed, upgraded and removed cleanly.
create-a-solution-aware-data-model.fullDescription: Tables created from the Tables page land in the Default solution with a random prefix and no clear path to production. Building the data model inside your own unmanaged solution, with your own publisher, keeps every component traceable and deployable as a managed solution.
create-a-solution-aware-data-model.problemStatement: A working app cannot be moved to production because its tables were created outside a solution, use the default prefix and drag in components nobody recognises.
whenToUse: Starting any Dataverse project that will be deployed to another environment
Splitting a large system into several solutions
Recovering a data model that was built in the Default solution
whenNotToUse: Experiments in a personal developer environment that will be thrown away
Dataverse for Teams environments, which manage tables through the Teams app instead of solutions you deploy
create-a-solution-aware-data-model.formulaOrCode:
Set-up
  1. Publisher           Contoso (prefix contoso, option value prefix 10000)
  2. Solution            Contoso Requests - Core      (publisher Contoso)
  3. Preferred solution  Solutions > Set preferred solution > Contoso Requests - Core
                         New components made anywhere in the maker portal now land in it.

Create components from inside the solution
  Solution > New > Table | Choice | App | Automation > Cloud flow | Security role |
  More > Environment variable | Connection reference

Adding existing tables (system or other publishers' tables)
  Add existing > Table > choose the table, then select only what you changed:
    "Include all objects"       No, unless you own the table
    "Include table metadata"    only if you changed table-level settings
    Select components           the columns, views and forms you added or changed
  Adding everything from Account or Contact makes your solution own, and later overwrite,
  components it never touched.

Suggested split for larger systems
  Contoso Core          publisher's tables, global choices, security roles
  Contoso Requests App  apps, forms, views, site map for one app            (depends on Core)
  Contoso Requests Flows   cloud flows, connection references, environment variables
  Start with one solution. Split only when teams or release cadences differ.

Managed properties (set before the first managed export)
  Table > Managed properties: can customers add forms, views, columns? Usually allow.

Check dependencies before export
  Solution > ... > Show dependencies, and Solution checker > Run.
  Missing dependencies listed at import are components referenced but not included or not
  present in the target.

Export
  Development   unmanaged, kept in source control
  Test / Prod   managed
  pac solution export --name ContosoRequestsCore --path ./out/ContosoRequestsCore_managed.zip --managed
  pac solution unpack --zipfile ./out/ContosoRequestsCore.zip --folder ./src/ContosoRequestsCore

Rescue: tables already built in the Default solution
  Same environment: Add existing > Table brings them into your solution, but the prefix stays.
  To fix the prefix, recreate the tables under your publisher and migrate the data with a dataflow.
stepByStepInstructions: Create the publisher and the solution.
Set the solution as your preferred solution.
Create tables, choices and roles from inside the solution.
When adding system tables, include only the components you changed.
Run solution checker and review dependencies.
Export as managed for test and production, and keep the unmanaged source in source control.
commonMistakes: Creating tables from the Tables page before a solution exists.
Adding a system table with all objects included.
Importing unmanaged solutions into production.
Several makers each using a different publisher in one project.
troubleshooting: If import fails with missing dependencies, add the listed components to the solution or install the solution that provides them first.
If a new table has a random prefix, it was created in the Default solution. Recreate it inside your solution.
If changes do not appear after a managed import, an unmanaged layer in the target sits on top. Remove the active customizations on that component.
If a solution cannot be deleted, another solution depends on it. Check Show dependencies.

faqs.question: Why should Dataverse tables be created inside a solution?
faqs.answer: A solution gives tables your publisher prefix and lets them be exported, deployed as managed, upgraded and removed as a unit. Tables made outside one get a default prefix and are hard to move.

faqs.question: What is a preferred solution?
faqs.answer: A setting that tells the maker portal which solution should receive new components you create outside a solution, instead of the Default solution.

faqs.question: Should I add all objects when including an existing table?
faqs.answer: No. Include only the columns, forms and views you created or changed. Including everything makes your solution take ownership of components it did not alter.

create-a-model-driven-app-sitemap.shortDescription: Plan and build the navigation of a model-driven app: areas, groups and subareas that match how each role works, with the right default views.
create-a-model-driven-app-sitemap.fullDescription: The site map is the left-hand navigation of a model-driven app. A good one is short, organised by task instead of by table, and hides what a role does not need. Planning it on paper first takes ten minutes and saves rebuilding the app designer layout later.
create-a-model-driven-app-sitemap.problemStatement: The app lists every table in one long group in the order they were created, so users cannot find the three things they use every day.
whenToUse: Building a new model-driven app
When users say they cannot find things
Combining several tables into one role-based app
whenNotToUse: Canvas apps, which have their own navigation
Single-table apps where one view is the whole experience
create-a-model-driven-app-sitemap.formulaOrCode:
Plan (example: Requests app)
  Area: Requests                     (shown as a switcher at the bottom of the navigation)
    Group: My work
      Dashboard        Request overview                         (default landing page)
      Subarea          My Active Requests      table: Service Request, default view: My Active Requests
      Subarea          My Tasks                table: Request Task
    Group: Team
      Subarea          Awaiting Review         table: Service Request (view set as default for reviewers)
      Subarea          All Open Requests
    Group: Reference
      Subarea          Categories              table: Request Category
  Area: Administration               (visible to admins only)
    Group: Setup
      Subarea          Environment settings    URL or custom page
      Subarea          Audit summary

Rules of thumb
  One area if there are fewer than about ten links. Areas add a click.
  Groups are named by task ("My work"), not by technology ("Tables").
  Five to seven links per group.
  Put the most used link first. It becomes the landing page unless a dashboard is set.
  The same table can appear more than once, each time with a different default view.

Build it (modern app designer)
  make.powerapps.com > Solutions > your solution > open the app > Edit
  Navigation pane: + Add page > Dataverse table | Dashboard | Custom page | URL | Web resource
  Select a group or page to rename it. Drag to reorder.
  Settings > Navigation: enable Areas, Collapsible groups, Home, Recent and Pinned as needed.
  For each table page: choose which forms and views the app includes, and the default view.

Different navigation per role
  Subareas for a table are hidden automatically when the user's roles give no read access to it.
  For finer control, edit the site map in the classic designer and set Privileges on a subarea,
  or build a second app for administrators and share each app with its own role.

Custom pages and URLs
  Custom page   a canvas-style page inside the app, for a landing page or wizard.
  URL           link to a report or SharePoint site. Opens in a new tab.

After changes
  Save, then Publish. Users see the change after a refresh.
  The app, its site map and the tables' forms and views must all be in the solution.
stepByStepInstructions: List the tasks each role performs daily and weekly.
Group tasks under two to four headings.
Sketch areas, groups and subareas, and choose a default view for each.
Add the pages in the app designer and rename groups.
Select only the forms and views each table needs in this app.
Publish and test signed in as each role.
commonMistakes: One group containing every table in the system.
Leaving all views and forms selected, so users face a long view list.
Naming groups after tables or teams instead of tasks.
Forgetting to publish after saving.
troubleshooting: If a subarea is missing for a user, their security role has no read privilege on that table.
If navigation changes do not show, publish the app and refresh the browser.
If the app opens on the wrong page, move the intended page to the top or set a default dashboard.
If the site map is missing after import, the app's site map component was not included in the solution.

faqs.question: What is a site map in a model-driven app?
faqs.answer: It is the app's navigation: areas at the top level, groups inside areas, and subareas that open a table view, dashboard, custom page or link.

faqs.question: How do I hide a navigation item from some users?
faqs.answer: Remove their read access to the table through security roles and the link hides itself, or set privileges on the subarea in the classic site map designer.

faqs.question: Can the same table appear twice in the navigation?
faqs.answer: Yes. Add it as two pages and give each a different default view, such as My Active Requests and Awaiting Review.

create-a-sharepoint-to-dataverse-migrati.shortDescription: A staged plan for moving an app's data from SharePoint lists to Dataverse: when it is worth it, how columns map, how to load the data and how to switch the app over.
create-a-sharepoint-to-dataverse-migrati.fullDescription: SharePoint lists are a good start, but apps outgrow them when they need row-level security, relationships, larger volumes or server-side rules. Migration goes best in stages: decide, map, build the tables, load and reconcile the data, rework the app and flows, then cut over with a rollback plan.
create-a-sharepoint-to-dataverse-migrati.problemStatement: Teams either stay on SharePoint long after it has become a liability or attempt a weekend migration with no mapping, losing person fields, attachments and history.
whenToUse: Lists near or past the 5,000 item view threshold with complex filters
Apps needing security by row, role or column
Data with several related lists and lookups
When licensing for Dataverse is in place
whenNotToUse: Document-centric solutions, which belong in libraries
Small lists with simple permissions and no licence budget for premium
create-a-sharepoint-to-dataverse-migrati.formulaOrCode:
1. Decide
  Signals to move: delegation workarounds everywhere, item-level permissions by flow, more than
  three related lists, audit requirements, more than ~50,000 rows, need for business rules.
  Cost: Dataverse is premium. Every user of the app needs Power Apps Premium or per-app licences.

2. Map columns
  SharePoint                    Dataverse
  Title                         primary name column (or Text)
  Single line / Multiple lines  Text / Multiline text
  Choice                        Choice (global where shared)
  Choice (multi)                Choices
  Number / Currency             Whole number or Decimal / Currency
  Date and time                 Date only or Date and time (set time zone behaviour deliberately)
  Yes/No                        Yes/No
  Person                        Lookup to User (match on email)       external people: Contact
  Person (multi)                many-to-many to User, or a child table
  Lookup                        Lookup (load parent table first)
  Managed metadata              Choice or lookup to a reference table
  Calculated                    Formula column
  Hyperlink                     Text with URL format
  Attachments                   Notes (annotation) attachments, or a File column
  Created / Created By          custom columns Original Created On / By, or override Created On on import
  Version history               not migrated; export it if it must be kept
  ID                            keep as Legacy SharePoint ID (whole number, alternate key)

3. Build the Dataverse tables in a solution, including the Legacy SharePoint ID key.

4. Load the data with a dataflow
  make.powerapps.com > Dataflows > New > SharePoint Online list > transform > Load to existing table
  Map the alternate key so re-running the dataflow updates instead of duplicating.
  Order: reference tables, then parents, then children.
  Person columns: map the email to the User table's Primary Email (domain name) key.
  Attachments need a flow: Get attachments > Get attachment content > Add a new row (Notes) or Upload a file.

5. Reconcile
  Row counts per list and table, sums of amount columns, counts per status, ten spot-checked rows.

6. Rework the app and flows
  Canvas app: add the Dataverse tables, replace each data source, fix choice and lookup syntax:
    SharePoint   Status.Value = "Open"          { Status: { Value: "Open" } }
    Dataverse    Status = 'Status'.Open         { Status: 'Status'.Open }
  Flows: replace SharePoint triggers and actions with Dataverse ones
  (When a row is added, modified or deleted; List rows; Update a row).

7. Cut over
  Freeze the lists (read-only permissions), run the dataflow one last time, reconcile,
  publish the new app, redirect links, keep the lists read-only for an agreed period, then archive.

Rollback: restore edit permissions on the lists and republish the previous app version.
stepByStepInstructions: Confirm the reasons to move and the licensing.
Map every column and decide what happens to people, attachments and history.
Build the tables with a legacy ID alternate key.
Create dataflows for reference data, parents and children, and run them into a test environment.
Reconcile counts and totals.
Rework the app and flows against Dataverse and test with real users.
Freeze, do the final load, cut over and keep the lists read-only as a fallback.
commonMistakes: Migrating without checking that users are licensed for premium connectors.
Loading child rows before their parents exist.
No alternate key, so a second run duplicates every row.
Forgetting attachments and person fields until after cut-over.
troubleshooting: If person lookups load empty, the email does not match a user in the environment. Add the users or map to Contact.
If the dataflow creates duplicates, map the alternate key in the load settings.
If dates shift by a day, the Dataverse column uses User Local behaviour. Use Date Only or Time Zone Independent for dates without a time.
If Created On shows the migration date, map the original date to the overriddencreatedon column during import or keep it in a custom column.

faqs.question: When should I move from SharePoint lists to Dataverse?
faqs.answer: When the app needs row or column-level security, real relationships, server-side rules, auditing or large volumes, and the users can be licensed for premium.

faqs.question: How do I migrate SharePoint list data to Dataverse?
faqs.answer: Use a Power Apps dataflow that reads the list and loads an existing Dataverse table, with an alternate key so it can be re-run. Attachments need a separate flow.

faqs.question: Do I need to rebuild my canvas app?
faqs.answer: The screens can stay, but every data source, filter and Patch needs updating because Dataverse choice and lookup syntax differs from SharePoint.

create-a-solution-layering-checklist.shortDescription: Understand and check solution layers in Dataverse so managed updates take effect and unmanaged changes in production do not hide them.
create-a-solution-layering-checklist.fullDescription: Every component in an environment is the sum of layers: the system layer, each managed solution in install order, and one unmanaged layer on top. The top layer wins. This checklist helps you design which solution owns what, and find the layer that explains why a deployed change is not showing.
create-a-solution-layering-checklist.problemStatement: A fix is deployed to production in a managed solution, the import succeeds, and the old behaviour remains because an unmanaged change made directly in production sits on top.
whenToUse: Before splitting a system into several solutions
When a deployed change does not appear in the target environment
Before every production release, as a gate
whenNotToUse: Single-environment personal apps with no deployments
Environments that only ever hold unmanaged solutions, such as a developer sandbox
create-a-solution-layering-checklist.formulaOrCode:
How layers stack (top wins)
  Unmanaged layer ("Active")          any change made directly in the environment
  Managed solution C                  installed last
  Managed solution B
  Managed solution A                  installed first
  System                              Microsoft's base

  Most properties: top layer wins.
  Some merge across layers: forms, site maps, model-driven app components.

See the layers of a component
  Solutions > open the solution > select the component > ... > Advanced > See solution layers
  The list shows each solution, its publisher and order. Open a layer to see the changed properties.

Remove an unmanaged layer in test or production
  See solution layers > select the Active layer > Remove active customizations
  This discards the direct change and reveals the managed version beneath. It cannot be undone,
  so copy anything that should be kept into development first.

Design checklist
  [ ] One publisher for all of your solutions
  [ ] Development is the only environment with unmanaged solutions
  [ ] Test and production receive managed solutions only
  [ ] Makers have no System Customizer role in test or production
  [ ] Each component is owned by exactly one of your solutions
  [ ] Shared components (tables, global choices) live in a base solution installed first
  [ ] Solutions that depend on the base are installed after it, always in the same order
  [ ] When adding system tables, only changed subcomponents are included
  [ ] No Active layer exists on your components in test or production (check before each release)

Release gate: find unmanaged layers quickly
  Solutions > Default Solution is not a reliable guide. Instead, for each key component
  (main forms, views, flows, apps) open See solution layers and confirm the top layer is managed.
  Scripted check (Web API): component layers for one component
  GET /api/data/v9.2/msdyn_componentlayers?$filter=msdyn_componentid eq '<component id>' and msdyn_solutioncomponentname eq 'SystemForm'

Update, upgrade or patch
  Update    replaces the managed layer's contents; components removed from the solution stay behind
  Upgrade   installs the new version and deletes components no longer in the solution (default, recommended)
  Stage for upgrade   install the new version alongside, apply the upgrade later
  Patch     a small solution containing only changed components, rolled into the next full version

Flows and apps
  Editing a managed flow in production creates an unmanaged layer on that flow.
  Turning a flow on or off does not.
stepByStepInstructions: Draw your solutions in install order with the base solution at the bottom.
Confirm every solution uses the same publisher.
Restrict customisation rights in test and production.
Before each release, check key components for an Active layer in the target.
Remove active customizations after copying any wanted change back to development.
Import with Upgrade so removed components are cleaned up.
commonMistakes: Fixing something quickly in production, which creates an unmanaged layer that blocks later releases.
Two solutions both containing the same form or view.
Importing solutions in a different order in different environments.
Using Update for every release, leaving deleted components behind.
troubleshooting: If a deployed change is not visible, open See solution layers on the component and look for an Active layer on top.
If a form shows fields from an older version, forms merge across layers. Remove the active layer or the older solution's customisation.
If an upgrade fails because a component is in use, another solution or an unmanaged component depends on it. Check dependencies.
If a managed flow shows as edited, someone changed it in the target. Remove the active layer to restore the deployed definition.

faqs.question: What is a solution layer in Power Platform?
faqs.answer: Each managed solution and the unmanaged customisations in an environment form layers on a component. The top layer decides what users see.

faqs.question: Why did my managed solution update not change anything?
faqs.answer: An unmanaged change made directly in that environment is sitting above your managed layer. Remove the active customizations on the component.

faqs.question: What is the difference between update and upgrade?
faqs.answer: Update overwrites the solution's components but leaves removed ones in place. Upgrade also deletes components that are no longer part of the solution.

create-a-deployment-readiness-review.shortDescription: A go or no-go review to run before a solution is imported to production: scope, testing, configuration, access, support and rollback.
create-a-deployment-readiness-review.fullDescription: Most failed Power Platform releases fail for ordinary reasons: a missing connection, an environment variable still pointing at test, a flow left off, or users without a licence. A thirty-minute readiness review with a fixed list of questions catches these before the import.
create-a-deployment-readiness-review.problemStatement: Releases go out on a Friday afternoon with no smoke test, no named owner and no way back, and Monday starts with a broken app.
whenToUse: Before every production import
When a new team takes over releases
After an incident caused by a deployment
whenNotToUse: Deployments to development or sandbox environments used for experiments
Emergency fixes already covered by a separate, shorter hotfix checklist
create-a-deployment-readiness-review.formulaOrCode:
Deployment readiness review

Release
  Solution(s) and version:            Contoso Requests 1.4.0.0
  Change summary / release notes:     linked
  Requested by / approved by:         named people
  Planned window and duration:        date, time, expected minutes
  Deployer (service account or pipeline):

Scope and quality
  [ ] Every item in the release is linked to a request or defect
  [ ] Solution checker run, no critical or high issues
  [ ] Tested in the test environment using the managed solution, not unmanaged
  [ ] User acceptance signed off by the business owner
  [ ] Tested with a non-admin account for each security role
  [ ] Accessibility and mobile checked where relevant

Configuration
  [ ] Environment variable values for production confirmed (see the register)
  [ ] Connection references mapped to production connections owned by the service account
  [ ] Deployment settings file reviewed
  [ ] DLP policy in production allows every connector used
  [ ] Required licences assigned to users (premium connectors, per-app passes)
  [ ] Security roles, teams and app sharing ready
  [ ] Reference data and data migration steps scripted and rehearsed

Target environment
  [ ] No unmanaged layers on components in this release
  [ ] Dependencies (base solutions) present at the required version
  [ ] Backup: note the latest system backup time, or take a manual backup immediately before import
  [ ] Storage capacity sufficient

Go-live
  [ ] Smoke test steps written (five to ten checks, named tester)
  [ ] Flows to turn on after import are listed, with their order
  [ ] Communication to users drafted (what changes, when, who to contact)
  [ ] Support team briefed, known issues listed

Rollback
  [ ] Trigger agreed: which failure means roll back, and who decides
  [ ] Method: restore the pre-import backup, or re-import the previous managed version
  [ ] Data created after go-live: how it is kept or re-entered

Decision
  Go | Go with conditions | No-go        Signed: business owner, technical owner, support owner

After the release
  Smoke test passed at:       Flows on:       Users notified:       Review notes:
stepByStepInstructions: Copy the review into your release record for each deployment.
Fill in the release details and link the release notes.
Walk through each section with the technical, business and support owners.
Resolve or accept every unticked item.
Record the decision and the names of those who made it.
After go-live, record the smoke test result and anything to improve.
commonMistakes: Testing the unmanaged solution and deploying the managed one untested.
Assuming connections and environment variables will sort themselves out at import.
No named person with authority to call a rollback.
Skipping the review for small changes.
troubleshooting: If the import fails on missing dependencies, install the required base solution version first.
If flows are off after import, their connection references had no connection. Map them and turn the flows on.
If users cannot open the app after release, check sharing, security roles and licences in that order.
If the app shows test data sources, an environment variable kept its old current value. Update it and restart the flows.

faqs.question: What should be checked before deploying a Power Platform solution to production?
faqs.answer: That it was tested as a managed solution, that environment variables and connections are set for production, that users have access and licences, and that a smoke test and rollback plan exist.

faqs.question: Should I back up before importing a solution?
faqs.answer: Yes. Production environments have automatic backups, and you can take a manual one just before import to have a known restore point.

faqs.question: Who should sign off a deployment?
faqs.answer: The business owner for scope and acceptance, the technical owner for the build and configuration, and the support owner for readiness to run it.

create-a-connection-reference-inventory.shortDescription: List every connection reference in a solution with its connector, the account behind it in each environment and the flows and apps that use it.
create-a-connection-reference-inventory.fullDescription: A connection reference is a pointer that flows and apps use instead of a connection. Each environment maps the pointer to its own connection. An inventory shows which account each one should use in production and which components break if that account is disabled.
create-a-connection-reference-inventory.problemStatement: A solution has eleven connection references for SharePoint because each maker's flow created its own, and half of them point at personal accounts in production.
whenToUse: Before the first deployment of a solution with flows
When moving flows from personal accounts to a service account
During an access review or when a maker leaves
whenNotToUse: Flows outside solutions, which use connections directly and should be moved into a solution first
Canvas apps where each user signs in with their own connection and no shared account is involved
create-a-connection-reference-inventory.formulaOrCode:
Inventory
  Display name                 Logical name                  Connector          Dev account        Prod account          Used by
  SharePoint - Requests        contoso_SharePointRequests    SharePoint         maker@contoso      svc-requests@contoso  Approval flow, Reminder flow, Request app
  Outlook - Notifications      contoso_OutlookNotify         Office 365 Outlook maker@contoso      svc-requests@contoso  Approval flow, Error handler
  Approvals                    contoso_Approvals             Approvals          maker@contoso      svc-requests@contoso  Approval flow
  Teams - Alerts               contoso_TeamsAlerts           Microsoft Teams    maker@contoso      svc-requests@contoso  High risk alert
  Dataverse                    contoso_Dataverse             Dataverse          maker@contoso      svc-requests@contoso  Sync flow

Rules
  One connection reference per connector per purpose, shared by all flows in the solution.
  Name it  <Connector> - <purpose>.  The default names (SharePoint-1a2b3) tell nobody anything.
  Production connections belong to a service account with the licences and permissions it needs.
  Record the account, never its password.

Find duplicates
  Solution > filter by Connection references. Several rows for the same connector usually mean
  each flow created its own. Edit each flow, switch its actions to the shared reference
  (action > ... > select the connection reference), then delete the unused ones.

Which flows use a reference
  Solution > connection reference > ... > Show dependencies
  Web API:
  GET /api/data/v9.2/connectionreferences?$select=connectionreferencedisplayname,connectionreferencelogicalname,connectorid,connectionid

Deployment settings file section
  "ConnectionReferences": [
    {
      "LogicalName": "contoso_SharePointRequests",
      "ConnectionId": "shared-sharepointonl-1a2b3c4d-....",
      "ConnectorId": "/providers/Microsoft.PowerApps/apis/shared_sharepointonline"
    }
  ]
  The ConnectionId is the last part of the connection's URL in the target environment:
  make.powerautomate.com > Connections > open the connection > copy the id from the address.

Who must own what
  The account importing the solution needs access to the connections it maps (own them, or have
  them shared). Service principals can own connections for connectors that support them,
  such as Dataverse.

Canvas apps
  Apps in solutions also use connection references for some connectors. Users of the app still
  sign in with their own connections unless the data source is shared implicitly (for example SQL
  with a fixed login), so review those separately.
stepByStepInstructions: Open the solution and list its connection references.
Merge duplicates so each connector and purpose has one reference.
Rename references to say what they are for.
Create the production connections under the service account.
Record connection ids and build the deployment settings file.
Review the inventory whenever a flow is added or an owner changes.
commonMistakes: Letting each new flow create its own connection reference.
Mapping production references to a maker's personal connection.
Deleting a connection that references still point at.
Leaving default names such as SharePoint-9f3a1.
troubleshooting: If flows are off after import, their connection references were not mapped. Open each reference, pick a connection and turn the flows on.
If import fails saying the connection is not found, the importing account cannot see the connection. Share it or import as its owner.
If a flow fails with unauthorised errors, the service account lost its licence, password or permissions on the data source.
If a reference cannot be deleted, a flow or app still depends on it. Check Show dependencies.

faqs.question: What is a connection reference in Power Automate?
faqs.answer: It is a solution component that points to a connection. Flows use the reference, and each environment maps it to its own connection, so flows do not need editing after deployment.

faqs.question: How many connection references should a solution have?
faqs.answer: One per connector and purpose. All flows that use SharePoint for the same job should share a single reference.

faqs.question: Who should own production connections?
faqs.answer: A service account, not an individual maker, so flows keep running when people change roles or leave.

create-an-unmanaged-customizations-clean.shortDescription: Find and remove unmanaged changes in test and production environments so managed deployments behave predictably again.
create-an-unmanaged-customizations-clean.fullDescription: Unmanaged customisations in downstream environments come from quick fixes, experiments and solutions that were once imported unmanaged. They override managed layers and make each environment slightly different. A cleanup plan inventories them, decides what to keep, moves keepers back into source and removes the rest.
create-an-unmanaged-customizations-clean.problemStatement: Production no longer matches development: forms differ, a flow was edited in place, and each release produces surprises nobody can reproduce in test.
whenToUse: Production and test behave differently for the same solution version
Before adopting pipelines or automated deployment
After inheriting an environment that was customised directly
whenNotToUse: Development environments, where unmanaged is the normal state
Environments about to be retired, where rebuilding from managed solutions is quicker than cleaning
create-an-unmanaged-customizations-clean.formulaOrCode:
1. Inventory what is unmanaged in the target
  a. Unmanaged solutions:  Solutions > filter Managed = No  (other than Default and Common Data Services Default)
  b. Unmanaged layers on managed components:
     open key components > Advanced > See solution layers > look for "Active" at the top
  c. Components that exist only unmanaged: Default Solution > filter each type by Managed = No
  d. Web API list of unmanaged solutions:
     GET /api/data/v9.2/solutions?$filter=ismanaged eq false and isvisible eq true&$select=friendlyname,uniquename,version

2. Classify each finding
  Finding                                     Decision
  Change that should exist everywhere         Recreate in development, deploy as managed, then remove the unmanaged copy
  Emergency fix already superseded            Remove active customizations
  Experiment or abandoned component           Delete
  Whole unmanaged solution in production      Convert: see step 4
  Data, not customisation (reference rows)    Leave; move to a configuration data process

3. Remove unmanaged layers
  Component > See solution layers > Active layer > Remove active customizations
  Test in a copy of production first. Removal cannot be undone.

4. Convert an unmanaged solution in production to managed
  a. Make sure development holds the same components (import the unmanaged solution there if needed).
  b. Export from development as managed, same unique name and publisher, higher version.
  c. Import the managed solution to production. Components become managed and keep their data.
     Unmanaged copies of the components remain as an Active layer.
  d. Remove active customizations on those components, or use
     "Convert to managed" during import (Advanced settings) where available so the Active layers
     are removed for you.
  e. Delete the old unmanaged solution container. Deleting an unmanaged solution removes only the
     container, not its components.

5. Prevent it returning
  [ ] Remove System Customizer and System Administrator from makers in test and production
  [ ] Enable "Block unmanaged customizations" in the environment's settings (Features) for production
  [ ] Deploy only through a pipeline or a service account
  [ ] Emergency fix process: fix in development, fast-track through test, deploy managed

Order of work
  Start with flows and apps (highest risk), then forms and views, then tables and columns.
  Do one solution per maintenance window and smoke test after each.
stepByStepInstructions: Copy production to a sandbox to rehearse the cleanup.
List unmanaged solutions, active layers and unmanaged-only components.
Classify each item with its owner.
Recreate anything worth keeping in development and deploy it as managed.
Remove active customizations and delete abandoned components in the rehearsal environment, then test.
Repeat in production in a maintenance window.
Turn on the block for unmanaged customizations and restrict roles.
commonMistakes: Removing active layers in production without rehearsing in a copy.
Deleting an unmanaged solution and assuming its components were removed.
Cleaning up without changing who has customisation rights, so the problem returns.
Trying to fix the whole environment in one window.
troubleshooting: If removing an active layer changes behaviour users relied on, the fix lived only in production. Restore from the rehearsal notes into development and redeploy.
If a component cannot be deleted, something depends on it. Use Show dependencies and remove the dependants first.
If import says the solution is already installed as unmanaged, import the managed version over it with the same unique name and remove the active layers afterwards.
If blocked customisation stops an urgent change, an administrator can lift the setting briefly, but record why.

faqs.question: How do I find unmanaged customizations in production?
faqs.answer: List unmanaged solutions, check See solution layers on key components for an Active layer, and filter the Default Solution for components that are not managed.

faqs.question: Does deleting an unmanaged solution remove its components?
faqs.answer: No. It removes only the solution container. The components stay in the environment and must be deleted individually.

faqs.question: Can I stop people customising production directly?
faqs.answer: Yes. Remove customiser roles from makers and enable the environment setting that blocks unmanaged customizations.

create-a-release-notes-template.shortDescription: A release notes template for Power Platform solutions that tells users what changed and gives support the version, configuration and rollback details.
create-a-release-notes-template.fullDescription: Release notes serve two readers. Users want to know what is new and what they must do differently. Support wants the version number, components changed, configuration steps and known issues. One short document with both parts, written for every release, also builds the change history auditors ask for.
create-a-release-notes-template.problemStatement: Users discover changes by accident, and three months later nobody can say which release introduced a behaviour or what version production is running.
whenToUse: Every deployment to production, however small
Handing a solution to a support team
Apps under audit or change control
whenNotToUse: Daily builds to development environments
Configuration-only changes such as updating a reference list row, which belong in a change log
create-a-release-notes-template.formulaOrCode:
Release notes: Contoso Requests

Version         1.4.0.0                      (major.minor.build.revision, matches the solution version)
Release date    20 November 2026
Environment     Production
Released by     service account / pipeline run link
Approved by     business owner

For users
  What is new
    - You can now save a request as a draft and submit it later.
    - Approvers get a reminder after three days.
  What has changed
    - The Category list is shorter. "Hardware" and "Devices" are now "Equipment".
  Fixed
    - Requests with attachments over 10 MB no longer fail to submit.
  What you need to do
    - Nothing. Open the app as usual. If it looks unchanged, refresh the page.
  Known issues
    - The reminder email shows times in UTC. A fix is planned for 1.4.1.
  Help
    - support@contoso.com

For support and administrators
  Solutions deployed
    Contoso Requests Core     1.3.2.0 -> 1.4.0.0     managed, upgrade
    Contoso Requests Flows    1.3.0.0 -> 1.4.0.0     managed, upgrade
  Components changed
    Tables      Service Request: new column Submitted On; Status reason value "Draft" added
    Apps        Request app (canvas): screens scrRequestForm, scrMyDrafts
    Flows       Approval flow (trigger condition changed), new flow "Approval reminder"
    Security    Role "Requester": no change
  Configuration
    Environment variables   new: Approval Reminder Days = 3
    Connection references   no change
    Data steps              ran script to rename categories (12 rows updated)
  Post-deployment steps
    Turned on "Approval reminder". Smoke test passed 18:40.
  Rollback
    Re-import Contoso Requests 1.3.x managed packages from the release store, or restore backup taken 17:55.
  Work items included
    REQ-212, REQ-219, BUG-87

Version numbering
  Major   breaking change or redesign          2.0.0.0
  Minor   new features                          1.4.0.0
  Build   fixes                                 1.4.1.0
  Revision  set by the pipeline per build       1.4.1.27

Where to publish
  Users: a pinned post in the team's channel, or a "What's new" screen in the app.
  Support: with the release record, next to the solution files.
stepByStepInstructions: Copy the template at the start of each release.
Fill in the user section in plain language, one line per change.
List the solutions, versions and components changed.
Record configuration, data steps and post-deployment actions as they are done.
Add known issues and the rollback method.
Publish the user section where users will see it and store the full notes with the release.
commonMistakes: Writing release notes for developers only, full of component names users do not recognise.
Not raising the solution version, so two different builds share a number.
Leaving out known issues.
Publishing notes somewhere users never look.
troubleshooting: If nobody can tell which version is live, check Solutions in the environment. The version column shows what is installed.
If users miss changes, add a short What's new dialog in the app that shows once per version.
If notes are skipped under time pressure, make them a required item in the deployment readiness review.
If versions drift between solutions, set them together in the pipeline.

faqs.question: What should Power Platform release notes include?
faqs.answer: For users: what is new, changed and fixed, anything they must do, and known issues. For support: solution versions, components changed, configuration and data steps, and how to roll back.

faqs.question: How should solution versions be numbered?
faqs.answer: Use major.minor.build.revision. Raise major for breaking changes, minor for features and build for fixes, and let the pipeline set the revision.

faqs.question: Where do I find the version installed in an environment?
faqs.answer: Open Solutions in the maker portal for that environment. Each solution shows its installed version.

create-a-maker-handoff-package.shortDescription: Everything a new owner needs to take over a Power Platform solution: access, architecture, configuration, known issues and a walkthrough.
create-a-maker-handoff-package.fullDescription: Makers move on. When they do, the apps and flows they built still run under their name and in their head. A handoff package moves ownership and knowledge together, in a fixed set of documents and access changes, so the next person can support the solution from day one.
create-a-maker-handoff-package.problemStatement: A maker changes role, their account is disabled a month later, and the flows they owned stop with nobody knowing what they did or where the data lives.
whenToUse: A maker is leaving or changing teams
A consultant is handing a build to the client
A citizen-built app is being adopted by IT
whenNotToUse: Personal productivity flows that end with the person
Solutions already run by a support team with current documentation and shared ownership
create-a-maker-handoff-package.formulaOrCode:
Handoff package

1. Summary (one page)
   Purpose, users, business owner, criticality, hours of use, what breaks for the business if it stops.

2. Inventory
   Environment(s) and URLs
   Solution name(s), publisher, current version
   Apps:   name, type, link, shared with
   Flows:  name, trigger, what it does, owner, connection references
   Data:   tables or lists, site URLs, approximate row counts
   Other:  Power BI reports, Teams channels, mailboxes, Key Vault

3. Architecture
   One diagram: users -> app -> data -> flows -> notifications and external systems.
   Data model: tables or lists, key columns, relationships, status values and what each means.

4. Configuration
   Environment variables and their values per environment
   Connection references and the accounts behind them
   Security: roles, groups, list permissions, who approves access
   Licences needed by users and by the service account
   DLP policy the environment is under

5. Operations
   How to deploy (pipeline or manual steps)
   Routine tasks: adding a category, onboarding an approver, month-end steps
   Monitoring: where failures show up, who is notified
   Known issues and workarounds
   Backlog of requested changes

6. Access to transfer
   [ ] Solution and environment: new owner has Environment Maker or System Customizer in development
   [ ] Apps: new owner added as co-owner
   [ ] Flows: new owner added as co-owner; primary owner changed where needed
   [ ] Connections: recreated under a service account or the new owner, and flows repointed
   [ ] SharePoint sites or Dataverse roles: new owner added
   [ ] Service account: credentials handed over through the password vault
   [ ] Source control and pipelines: access granted
   [ ] Shared mailbox, Teams channel, Power BI workspace: access granted

7. Walkthrough (recorded, about an hour)
   Demo as a user, open each flow and explain its purpose, show a deployment, show where it has failed before.

8. Sign-off
   Outgoing maker, incoming owner, business owner. Date the old owner's access can be removed.

Change the owner of a flow
  Solution flow: flow details > Edit > Owner. Or with PowerShell:
  Set-AdminFlowOwnerRole -EnvironmentName <env> -FlowName <flow id> -PrincipalType User -PrincipalObjectId <new owner object id> -RoleName CanEdit
Change the owner of a canvas app
  Set-AdminPowerAppOwner -AppName <app id> -EnvironmentName <env> -AppOwner <new owner object id>
stepByStepInstructions: Start the package at least two weeks before the maker leaves.
Build the inventory from the solution and the admin center, not from memory.
Draw the architecture and data model diagrams.
Transfer access item by item using the checklist.
Record the walkthrough.
Have the new owner make and deploy one small change while the previous owner is still available.
Sign off and schedule removal of the old access.
commonMistakes: Handing over documents without transferring ownership of flows and connections.
Leaving connections under the departing maker's account.
Skipping the first change by the new owner, which is the real test.
Describing what the solution does but not why decisions were made.
troubleshooting: If flows stop after the maker's account is disabled, their connections died with it. Recreate the connections under a service account and repoint the references.
If the new owner cannot edit a flow, they were added as a run-only user. Add them as an owner.
If an app shows the old owner, change it with Set-AdminPowerAppOwner.
If nobody knows what a flow does, check its run history inputs and outputs before changing it.

faqs.question: What happens to Power Automate flows when their owner leaves?
faqs.answer: They keep running until the owner's account or connections stop working. After that they fail. Add co-owners and move connections to a service account before the person leaves.

faqs.question: How do I change the owner of a canvas app?
faqs.answer: An administrator can run Set-AdminPowerAppOwner, or the owner can add co-owners from the app's Share dialog.

faqs.question: What should a handoff document include?
faqs.answer: The purpose and owners, an inventory of apps, flows and data, an architecture diagram, configuration and security details, operating procedures, known issues and the access that was transferred.

create-a-production-support-ownership-mo.shortDescription: Define who owns what once a Power Platform solution is live: business owner, technical owner, support tiers, service account, and what each is expected to do.
create-a-production-support-ownership-mo.fullDescription: A solution without named owners is supported by whoever built it, for as long as they are around. A simple ownership model names the business owner, the technical owner and a backup, sets out support tiers and response times, and records which account the solution runs under.
create-a-production-support-ownership-mo.problemStatement: When the app fails, users email the person who built it two years ago, who has moved teams, and nobody else has access or knows the priority.
whenToUse: Before go-live of any app more than one team depends on
When IT adopts maker-built solutions
After an outage with no clear owner
whenNotToUse: Personal apps and flows used only by their maker
Prototypes and pilots with an agreed end date and a single sponsor
create-a-production-support-ownership-mo.formulaOrCode:
Ownership record (one per solution)
  Solution                 Contoso Requests
  Criticality              High | Medium | Low        (drives response times)
  Business owner           decides priorities, approves changes and access      name
  Technical owner          accountable for the build and its health             name
  Backup technical owner   covers absence; has the same access                  name
  Support contact          how users ask for help                               support@contoso.com / Teams channel
  Service account          owns connections and flows in production             svc-requests@contoso.com
  Environment              Production - Operations
  Review date              every six months

Responsibilities (RACI)
  Activity                          Business owner  Technical owner  Support team  Platform admin
  Approve new features                    A               R               C              I
  Approve access requests                 A               I               R              I
  Fix defects                             I               A/R             R              C
  Deploy releases                         I               A/R             I              C
  Monitor flow failures                   I               A               R              I
  Licence and capacity                    C               C               I              A/R
  DLP and environment settings            I               C               I              A/R
  Renew service account credentials       I               A               R              C

Support tiers
  Tier 1  Service desk or super users    how-to questions, access requests, known issues list
  Tier 2  Technical owner or app team    defects, data fixes, flow failures
  Tier 3  Platform team or vendor        environment, connector, licensing or Microsoft issues

Response targets by criticality
              Acknowledge     Workaround or fix
  High        1 hour          same business day
  Medium      4 hours         3 business days
  Low         1 business day  next release

Minimum controls for a High solution
  [ ] At least two owners on every app and flow
  [ ] Runs under a service account with a non-expiring or monitored credential
  [ ] Flow failure notifications go to a shared mailbox or channel
  [ ] Runbook: how to check health, rerun a failed flow, fix common data problems
  [ ] In a managed solution, deployed by pipeline
  [ ] Listed in the flow and app inventory

Where to keep it
  A SharePoint list or Dataverse table with one row per solution, linked from the app's Help
  screen and from the service desk knowledge base.
stepByStepInstructions: Rate the solution's criticality with the business owner.
Name the business owner, technical owner and backup.
Agree support tiers and response targets.
Move connections and flow ownership to a service account.
Route failure notifications to a shared mailbox or channel.
Publish the record and link it from the app and the service desk.
Review it every six months and whenever a named person changes role.
commonMistakes: Naming a team instead of a person as owner.
No backup, so one holiday leaves the solution unsupported.
Failure emails going to an individual's inbox.
Agreeing response times the team cannot staff.
troubleshooting: If incidents bounce between teams, the tier boundaries are unclear. Add examples of what each tier handles.
If the owner list is out of date, tie the review to the six-monthly access review.
If the service account's password expiry stops flows, monitor the expiry date or use an account policy suited to service accounts.
If business owners will not prioritise, show them the open backlog and ask for the top three.

faqs.question: Who should own a Power Platform app in production?
faqs.answer: A business owner who decides priorities and access, and a technical owner with a named backup who is accountable for keeping it running.

faqs.question: Why use a service account for production flows?
faqs.answer: Flows run under their connections. A service account keeps them running when individual makers leave or lose licences.

faqs.question: How do I decide how much support an app needs?
faqs.answer: Rate its criticality by what stops if it fails and how many people are affected, then set response targets and controls to match.

create-a-rollback-decision-checklist.shortDescription: Decide before a release how you would undo it: which failures trigger a rollback, who decides, and which method applies to solutions, data and flows.
create-a-rollback-decision-checklist.fullDescription: Power Platform has no single undo button for a deployment. You can restore an environment backup, re-import the previous managed version, or fix forward. Each has different costs, especially for data created after go-live. Choosing in advance turns a stressful incident into a short, agreed procedure.
create-a-rollback-decision-checklist.problemStatement: A release breaks approvals, and the team spends two hours arguing about whether to restore, fix or wait while requests pile up.
whenToUse: Planning any production release
Releases that include schema or data changes
High-criticality solutions
whenNotToUse: Development and sandbox environments where a reset is acceptable
Brand-new solutions with no users yet, where uninstalling is always acceptable
create-a-rollback-decision-checklist.formulaOrCode:
Before the release
  [ ] Previous managed solution files (.zip) stored and labelled with their versions
  [ ] Backup: latest automatic backup time noted, or manual backup taken just before import
      Power Platform admin center > Environments > select > Backups > Create
  [ ] Rollback triggers agreed (below)
  [ ] Decision maker named, with a deputy
  [ ] Time limit: if the smoke test is not passing within N minutes, decide

Triggers
  Roll back                                    Fix forward
  Core process blocked for all users           Cosmetic or minor defect
  Data being written incorrectly               Workaround exists and is acceptable
  Security or permissions exposed              Affects a small group, fix is under an hour
  Smoke test fails and cause is unknown        Cause is known and isolated to one component

Methods
  Method                           Undoes                         Keeps new data?   Time      Notes
  A. Fix forward (hotfix)          the defect only                yes               varies    preferred when cause is known
  B. Turn off the new component    a new flow or feature flag     yes               minutes   needs feature switches built in
  C. Re-import previous managed    app, flow and form changes     yes               30-60 min cannot remove new columns that hold data;
     version                                                                                  import the older version as an upgrade
  D. Uninstall the new solution    everything it added            no, its tables    30+ min   only for brand-new solutions; deletes
                                                                  are deleted                 their tables and data
  E. Restore environment backup    everything, including data     no                1-2 hours restores to a point in time; data entered
                                                                                              after that point is lost unless exported

Things that do not roll back with a solution
  Data changes made by migration scripts or flows
  Rows users created or changed after go-live
  Emails, approvals and Teams messages already sent
  Changes in other systems (SharePoint lists, SQL)

Data safety steps for schema releases
  Export affected tables (or copy the SharePoint list) before running data scripts.
  Make data scripts re-runnable and write a reverse script.
  Prefer additive changes: add a column now, remove the old one a release later.

During an incident
  1. Stop the damage: turn off affected flows, or put the app into maintenance mode (a feature flag).
  2. Decision maker picks a method using the table.
  3. Tell users what is happening and when the next update will come.
  4. Execute, then run the smoke test.
  5. Record what happened and what would have caught it earlier.

Restore to a sandbox first
  For method E, restore the backup to a new sandbox environment when time allows, confirm it is
  the right point in time, and copy needed data out before restoring over production.
stepByStepInstructions: Store the previous solution version and confirm a backup before each release.
Agree triggers and the decision maker in the readiness review.
Classify the release: app only, schema change, or data change.
Pick the default rollback method for that class.
Write the first three steps for the incident on the release record.
After any rollback, hold a short review and update this checklist.
commonMistakes: Assuming an environment restore is quick and loses nothing.
Having no copy of the previous managed solution.
Deleting or renaming columns in the same release that stops using them.
Nobody empowered to make the call.
troubleshooting: If the previous version will not import, the newer one added components with data. Import as an upgrade and handle the extra columns separately.
If a restore is needed but the backup is older than expected, check the list of system backups. They are continuous for production environments with a retention period.
If flows resend notifications after a restore, turn flows off before restoring and review them before turning them on.
If data was changed wrongly, use auditing or the exported copy to rebuild the affected rows.

faqs.question: How do I roll back a Power Platform solution deployment?
faqs.answer: Either fix forward, re-import the previous managed version, or restore the environment from a backup. The right choice depends on whether data changed and how much new data would be lost.

faqs.question: Does restoring an environment backup lose data?
faqs.answer: Yes. Everything entered after the backup point is lost unless you export it first.

faqs.question: Can I uninstall a managed solution to undo a release?
faqs.answer: Only safely for a brand-new solution. Uninstalling deletes the tables it introduced along with their data.

create-a-managed-solution-promotion-path.shortDescription: Choose and document how solutions move from development to test to production: manual export and import, Power Platform pipelines, or Azure DevOps and GitHub.
create-a-managed-solution-promotion-path.fullDescription: A promotion path is the fixed route a solution takes to production and the rules along it: which environments, who can deploy, what is checked at each step, and where the solution files are kept. Picking the simplest route the team will follow consistently matters more than picking the most advanced.
create-a-managed-solution-promotion-path.problemStatement: Each release is done differently by whoever is available, sometimes skipping test, and production contains versions that were never tested as managed.
whenToUse: Setting up ALM for a new solution
Moving from manual imports to automated deployment
Standardising how several teams release
whenNotToUse: Apps that live in a single environment by design
Dataverse for Teams apps, which move by export and import within Teams
create-a-managed-solution-promotion-path.formulaOrCode:
The path
  Development (unmanaged)  ->  Test / UAT (managed)  ->  Production (managed)
  One direction only. Nothing is built or fixed in test or production.

Rules
  [ ] Development is the only place solutions are unmanaged
  [ ] The same managed file that passed test is the one imported to production
  [ ] Version number raised for every export
  [ ] Environment variables and connection references set per environment, not edited by hand in flows
  [ ] Deployments run under a service account or service principal
  [ ] Solution files or unpacked source kept in a repository or release store

Three ways to run it
                         Manual                 Power Platform pipelines        Azure DevOps / GitHub Actions
  Set-up effort          none                   low (install app, add stages)   medium to high
  Who it suits           one maker, few releases   maker teams, most projects   pro-dev teams, many solutions
  Source control         manual zip storage     optional (Git integration)      yes, unpacked source
  Approvals              by agreement           built in (delegated deployment, approval flows)   branch policies, environments
  Automated checks       solution checker by hand  pre-deployment checks via extensions   checker, tests, gates in the pipeline
  Licensing              none extra             target environments must be Managed Environments   as required by environments used

Manual
  Dev:  Solutions > select > Export > Managed (raise version) > store the zip
  Test: Solutions > Import > set connections and variables > Upgrade
  Prod: same file, same steps

Power Platform pipelines
  1. Install "Power Platform Pipelines" in a host environment.
  2. Deployment Pipeline Configuration app: add the development, test and production environments,
     create a pipeline with stages Test and Production, share it with makers.
  3. In development: Solutions > open solution > Pipelines > choose the Test stage > Deploy.
  4. After testing, deploy the same artifact to Production.
  Use delegated deployment with a service principal so makers do not need rights in production.

Azure DevOps (Power Platform Build Tools) outline
  Build:    Tool Installer -> Export Solution (unmanaged) -> Unpack -> commit
            -> Pack -> Checker -> Export or Pack managed -> publish artifact
  Release:  Import Solution (managed, settings file per stage) -> Apply Solution Upgrade
            -> activate flows -> smoke test
  GitHub:   microsoft/powerplatform-actions provides the same steps.

pac CLI equivalents
  pac solution export --name ContosoRequests --path out/ContosoRequests_managed.zip --managed
  pac solution check --path out/ContosoRequests_managed.zip
  pac solution import --path out/ContosoRequests_managed.zip --settings-file settings.test.json --stage-and-upgrade

Hotfix route
  Fix in development -> deploy to test -> short regression -> production. Same path, faster.
  If production must be patched first, repeat the change in development the same day.
stepByStepInstructions: Name the environments on the path and who may deploy to each.
Choose manual, pipelines or DevOps based on team size and release frequency.
Create the service account or service principal for deployments.
Prepare environment variable values and connections in test and production.
Run one full release along the path and write down every step that needed a human.
Store the released files and notes, and review the path after three releases.
commonMistakes: Exporting a fresh managed file for production instead of promoting the one that was tested.
Skipping test for small changes.
Deploying with personal accounts that later lose access.
Adopting a complex DevOps pipeline nobody on the team can maintain.
troubleshooting: If the pipeline option is missing in the solution, the environment is not linked to a pipeline or you lack the pipeline user role.
If a pipeline deployment fails on connections, the deploying identity cannot use them. Share the connections or pre-create them for that identity.
If import says a newer version is installed, raise the version in development and export again.
If test and production differ after the same file was imported, look for unmanaged layers in one of them.

faqs.question: What is the simplest way to deploy a Power Platform solution?
faqs.answer: Export it as managed from development and import that file to test, then to production. Power Platform pipelines automate the same steps with a few clicks.

faqs.question: Should I use Power Platform pipelines or Azure DevOps?
faqs.answer: Pipelines suit most maker teams and need little set-up. Azure DevOps or GitHub Actions fit teams that want source control, automated checks and complex release flows.

faqs.question: Why deploy managed solutions to production?
faqs.answer: Managed solutions can be upgraded and removed cleanly, protect components from direct edits and make each environment match what was tested.

create-an-environment-inventory.shortDescription: Keep a register of every Power Platform environment with its purpose, owner, type, region, security group and review date.
create-an-environment-inventory.fullDescription: The admin center lists environments but not why they exist or who answers for them. An inventory adds the missing facts: purpose, business owner, data sensitivity, DLP policy and whether the environment is still needed. It is the starting point for every other governance task.
create-an-environment-inventory.problemStatement: The tenant has dozens of environments named Test, Test2 and a former employee's name, and nobody can say which are safe to delete.
whenToUse: Starting governance in a tenant with more than a handful of environments
Before applying DLP policies or environment routing
Preparing for a licence, capacity or security review
whenNotToUse: Tenants with only the default environment and no plans for more
Tenants already running the CoE Starter Kit, which maintains this inventory for you
create-an-environment-inventory.formulaOrCode:
Inventory columns
  Display name            Operations - Production
  Environment ID          GUID
  URL                     https://contoso-ops.crm.dynamics.com
  Type                    Default | Production | Sandbox | Developer | Trial | Teams
  Purpose                 one sentence
  Stage                   Dev | Test | Prod | Personal | Training
  Business owner          person
  Technical owner         person, plus backup
  Region                  for example Europe
  Dataverse               Yes / No
  Managed Environment     Yes / No
  Security group          Entra ID group that limits who can be added
  DLP policy              policy name
  Data sensitivity        Public | Internal | Confidential
  Storage used (GB)       database / file / log
  Apps / Flows            counts
  Created on / by
  Last reviewed, Next review
  Status                  Active | Review | Scheduled for deletion

Fill it from the platform
  PowerShell (Microsoft.PowerApps.Administration.PowerShell)
    Add-PowerAppsAccount
    Get-AdminPowerAppEnvironment |
      Select-Object DisplayName, EnvironmentName, EnvironmentType,
        @{n="Region";e={$_.Location}}, CreatedTime,
        @{n="CreatedBy";e={$_.CreatedBy.displayName}},
        @{n="Url";e={$_.Internal.properties.linkedEnvironmentMetadata.instanceUrl}},
